title: The Bible · Books and data points
chronology: Books supply the narrative sequence, with overlapping historical settings. Each data point retains its own object, event, and recovery dates.
coverage: Includes all 1,285 verse-linked entries in the recorded OpenBible geographic snapshot, alongside archaeological, historical and manuscript data points. The wider collection continues to grow.

books.title: Genesis
books.periodLabel: Primeval origins; ancestors before the exodus
books.periodNote: The opening stories have no assigned absolute chronology. The ancestral narratives precede Israel's life in Egypt; their setting is distinct from the book's later formation.
books.summary: Creation, the flood and the nations lead into the stories of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph in Egypt.

sources.title: Introduction to Genesis (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Exodus
books.periodLabel: Egypt, the exodus and Sinai
books.periodNote: This is the narrative setting before settlement in Canaan. Proposed historical dates for the exodus remain debated; the book preserves traditions shaped over time.
books.summary: Moses leads Israel out of slavery, and the people enter a covenant at Sinai and build the tabernacle.

sources.title: Introduction to Exodus (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Leviticus
books.periodLabel: Israel's encampment at Sinai
books.periodNote: The laws are placed within the wilderness story. Their narrative setting does not provide a single date for the development or collection of these priestly traditions.
books.summary: Instructions for sacrifice, priesthood, purity and holiness describe worship and daily life within the covenant.

sources.title: Introduction to Leviticus (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Numbers
books.periodLabel: The wilderness journey from Sinai to Moab
books.periodNote: The book supplies an internal sequence of wilderness years, not an independently established absolute chronology. Its laws and narratives were collected over time.
books.summary: Israel travels, rebels and receives further instruction while an older generation gives way to the generation approaching Canaan.

sources.title: Introduction to Numbers (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Deuteronomy
books.periodLabel: Moses' final addresses before entering Canaan
books.periodNote: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab within the story. The book's composition and editing belong to later periods, including the monarchy and exile.
books.summary: Moses recalls the journey, restates covenant obligations and urges Israel to choose faithfulness before his death.

sources.title: Introduction to Deuteronomy (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Joshua
books.periodLabel: Entry into Canaan; before the monarchy
books.periodNote: The narrative follows the wilderness journey. Its relationship to settlement archaeology and absolute chronology is debated; the book took shape later than the events it portrays.
books.summary: Joshua leads Israel into Canaan, the land is allotted among the tribes, and the people renew their covenant.

sources.title: Introduction to Joshua (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Judges
books.periodLabel: Pre-monarchic Israel
books.periodNote: The stories belong to the period between Joshua and the monarchy, conventionally associated with early Iron Age Israel. Their arrangement is not a continuous, securely dated chronology.
books.summary: Recurring oppression and deliverance frame the stories of Israel's leaders, followed by episodes of tribal conflict.

sources.title: Introduction to Judges (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Ruth
books.periodLabel: The days of the judges
books.periodNote: The opening places the story before the monarchy. Its narrative setting is earlier than the book's composition, whose date remains uncertain.
books.summary: Ruth accompanies Naomi to Bethlehem, forms a household with Boaz, and becomes an ancestor of David.

sources.title: Introduction to Ruth (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 1 Samuel
books.periodLabel: The transition to kingship, late 11th–10th centuries BCE
books.periodNote: These are approximate conventional dates for the monarchy's beginnings. The book combines traditions about Samuel, Saul and David in a later edited narrative.
books.summary: Samuel guides Israel's transition to monarchy; Saul becomes king, and David rises as Saul's rule unravels.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Samuel (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 2 Samuel
books.periodLabel: David's reign, approximately the 10th century BCE
books.periodNote: The setting is David's kingship rather than the date of composition. Older accounts were shaped into the later narrative of Israel's monarchy.
books.summary: David establishes his kingdom in Jerusalem, receives a dynastic promise, and faces family violence, rebellion and the consequences of his actions.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Samuel (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 1 Kings
books.periodLabel: Solomon and the divided kingdoms, 10th–9th centuries BCE
books.periodNote: The narrative moves from David's death through Solomon to divided Israel and Judah. The books of Kings reached their later form in the setting of exile.
books.summary: Solomon builds the Temple; the kingdom divides, and royal histories intertwine with the ministry of Elijah.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Kings (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 2 Kings
books.periodLabel: Divided kingdoms to Babylonian exile, 9th–6th centuries BCE
books.periodNote: The story includes Samaria's fall in 722/721 BCE and Jerusalem's destruction in 587/586 BCE. Its ending reaches into the exile; these are narrative dates, not one composition date.
books.summary: Elisha's ministry and the histories of Israel and Judah culminate in conquest, Jerusalem's destruction, and deportation to Babylon.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Kings (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 1 Chronicles
books.periodLabel: Genealogies from origins; the reign of David
books.periodNote: The genealogies reach back to Adam, while the sustained narrative centers on David. This is a postexilic retelling of earlier traditions, not a continuously dated account.
books.summary: Genealogies introduce Israel's story, then David organizes worship and prepares for the Temple his son will build.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Chronicles (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 2 Chronicles
books.periodLabel: Solomon to exile and Cyrus, 10th–6th centuries BCE
books.periodNote: The narrative revisits earlier royal history from a postexilic perspective. Its closing proclamation of Cyrus opens the possibility of return.
books.summary: Solomon builds the Temple, Judah's kings alternate between reform and failure, and exile gives way to permission to return.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Chronicles (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Ezra
books.periodLabel: Persian-period restoration, 6th–5th centuries BCE
books.periodNote: The book combines return traditions, documents and Ezra's activity. Ezra's chronological relationship to Nehemiah is debated, so the sequence should not be treated as uniformly settled.
books.summary: Exiles return, rebuild the Temple, and address the community's identity and commitments through Ezra's teaching of the law.

sources.title: Introduction to Ezra (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Nehemiah
books.periodLabel: Jerusalem under Persian rule, 5th century BCE
books.periodNote: Nehemiah's first governorship is placed in 445–432 BCE under Artaxerxes I. His memoirs and other materials were brought together in the book's later form.
books.summary: Nehemiah rebuilds Jerusalem's walls, confronts opposition and inequality, and works with the community on covenant renewal and reform.

sources.title: Introduction to Nehemiah (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Esther
books.periodLabel: A Persian court in the 5th century BCE
books.periodNote: The story is set under Ahasuerus, associated with Xerxes I. The court setting is distinct from the book's later composition and does not establish every episode's historical chronology.
books.summary: Esther and Mordecai counter Haman's threat against the Jews, and the community commemorates its deliverance through Purim.

sources.title: Introduction to Esther (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Job
books.periodLabel: An undated world of household, suffering and wisdom
books.periodNote: The story has no secure historical date. The NABRE introduction places its literary composition broadly between the seventh and fifth centuries BCE; that is not the date of Job's life.
books.summary: Job loses family, health and prosperity, debates suffering with his companions, and encounters God in speeches about creation.

sources.title: Introduction to Job (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Psalms
books.periodLabel: Worship across monarchic, exilic and later Israel
books.periodNote: This anthology spans many settings and generations. Individual psalms and their collections have different histories; a superscription does not securely date every poem.
books.summary: Songs of praise, lament, thanksgiving, kingship and wisdom give voice to individual and communal prayer.

sources.title: Introduction to Psalms (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Proverbs
books.periodLabel: Wisdom across monarchic and later Israel
books.periodNote: The book gathers multiple collections, including sayings associated with Solomon and later compilers. It has no single narrative period or composition date.
books.summary: Sayings and extended instructions explore wisdom, work, speech, justice, family and the formation of character.

sources.title: Introduction to Proverbs (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Ecclesiastes
books.periodLabel: Wisdom reflection in a royal Jerusalem setting
books.periodNote: The speaker's royal persona evokes Solomon; it does not securely date the work to his reign. The book is commonly situated in the later postexilic, Hellenistic period.
books.summary: Qoheleth examines work, pleasure, injustice, mortality and the limits of human understanding while considering how life can be received.

sources.title: Introduction to Ecclesiastes (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Song of Songs
books.periodLabel: An undated world of lovers, gardens and royal imagery
books.periodNote: The poems do not narrate one historical period. Their association with Solomon differs from the question of composition, often placed in the postexilic period.
books.summary: A collection of love poetry gives voice to desire, mutual admiration, separation and reunion.

sources.title: Introduction to Song of Songs (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Isaiah
books.periodLabel: 8th-century Judah through exile and restoration
books.periodNote: The book contains several historical horizons: Assyrian-era Judah, the later Babylonian exile, and postexilic Jerusalem. These settings reflect a collection formed across generations.
books.summary: Judgment against injustice and unfaithfulness stands alongside visions of deliverance, restoration, a servant's mission, and renewed creation.

sources.title: Introduction to Isaiah (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Jeremiah
books.periodLabel: Judah's final decades and exile, late 7th–6th centuries BCE
books.periodNote: The settings run from Josiah's reign through Jerusalem's fall and its aftermath. The book's collection, editing and textual forms have a longer history.
books.summary: Jeremiah warns Judah, confronts rulers and prophets, witnesses national collapse, and announces hope through restoration and a renewed covenant.

sources.title: Introduction to Jeremiah (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Lamentations
books.periodLabel: Jerusalem's destruction and aftermath, 587/586 BCE
books.periodNote: These poems respond to the city's catastrophe rather than providing a daily chronicle. The circumstances of the individual poems and their collection need not be identical.
books.summary: Five poems grieve Jerusalem's devastation, wrestle with suffering and judgment, and appeal for divine attention and restoration.

sources.title: Introduction to Lamentations (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Ezekiel
books.periodLabel: The Babylonian exile, 6th century BCE
books.periodNote: The prophet's setting follows the deportation of 597 BCE and spans the period before and after Jerusalem's destruction. The dated visions do not fix every stage of the book's formation.
books.summary: Ezekiel's visions and symbolic actions announce judgment, then imagine renewed life, a restored people, and a transformed sanctuary.

sources.title: Introduction to Ezekiel (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Daniel
books.periodLabel: A 6th-century BCE court setting; visions of later empires
books.periodNote: The Babylonian and Persian court stories are set in the sixth century BCE. The book's final formation is widely placed in the second century BCE, especially the crisis under Antiochus IV.
books.summary: Daniel and his companions remain faithful under foreign kings, while visions interpret successive empires and anticipate divine deliverance.

sources.title: Introduction to Daniel (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Hosea
books.periodLabel: The northern kingdom's final decades, 8th century BCE
books.periodNote: Hosea's ministry belongs to Israel before Samaria's fall in 722/721 BCE. The collection's later transmission and editing are distinct from that prophetic setting.
books.summary: Images of marriage and family expose Israel's broken covenant while portraying judgment and the possibility of renewed love.

sources.title: Introduction to Hosea (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Joel
books.periodLabel: A crisis in Judah; probably a postexilic setting
books.periodNote: The book names no reigning king or securely dated event. Its Temple-centered community is often placed after the exile, but the precise date remains uncertain.
books.summary: A devastating locust crisis prompts lament and repentance, followed by promises of restoration, the Spirit, and judgment among the nations.

sources.title: Introduction to Joel (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Amos
books.periodLabel: The northern kingdom under Jeroboam II, 8th century BCE
books.periodNote: The main prophetic setting is Israel's monarchy before the Assyrian conquest. The collection's concluding restoration outlook and editorial history should not be reduced to one moment.
books.summary: Amos condemns injustice and complacent worship, announces judgment, and closes with a vision of restoration.

sources.title: Introduction to Amos (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Obadiah
books.periodLabel: Jerusalem's fall and its aftermath, 6th century BCE
books.periodNote: The denunciation of Edom is usually read against the catastrophe of 587/586 BCE. The exact date of the oracle and its collection is not certain.
books.summary: Edom is condemned for its conduct toward Judah, and Zion's eventual restoration reverses the experience of dispossession.

sources.title: Introduction to Obadiah (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Jonah
books.periodLabel: Assyrian Nineveh in an earlier prophetic world
books.periodNote: The story looks back to Assyria and an earlier prophet. Its literary composition is generally placed after the exile, so setting and writing date should be kept distinct.
books.summary: Jonah flees his commission, survives the sea, preaches to Nineveh, and protests when God spares its repentant people.

sources.title: Introduction to Jonah (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Micah
books.periodLabel: 8th-century Judah, with later restoration horizons
books.periodNote: The main prophetic setting is the Assyrian period; parts of the collection reflect exile and restoration. The entire book should not be assigned to one historical moment.
books.summary: Micah challenges exploitation and corrupt leadership, announces judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem, and envisions a restored community of peace.

sources.title: Introduction to Micah (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Nahum
books.periodLabel: Assyria's decline and Nineveh's fall, 7th century BCE
books.periodNote: The oracles anticipate Nineveh's destruction in 612 BCE. This anchors the historical horizon without providing one exact year for every part of the book.
books.summary: Poetry against Nineveh portrays the downfall of a violent imperial power as deliverance for peoples it oppressed.

sources.title: Introduction to Nahum (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Habakkuk
books.periodLabel: The Babylonian threat, late 7th–early 6th centuries BCE
books.periodNote: The dialogue belongs to the horizon of Babylon's rise. Its literary structure, including the concluding prayer, is distinct from a precisely dated sequence of events.
books.summary: Habakkuk questions violence and injustice, receives an answer about judgment, and responds with a prayer of trust.

sources.title: Introduction to Habakkuk (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Zephaniah
books.periodLabel: Judah under Josiah, late 7th century BCE
books.periodNote: The superscription places the prophet in Josiah's reign, 640–609 BCE. The book's judgment and restoration material need not all reflect one occasion.
books.summary: The day of the Lord brings judgment on Judah and the nations, followed by hope for a humble and restored people.

sources.title: Introduction to Zephaniah (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Haggai
books.periodLabel: Rebuilding the Jerusalem Temple, 520 BCE
books.periodNote: The dated oracles belong to the second year of Darius I. Their dates locate the prophet's activity, not necessarily every step in the collection's editing.
books.summary: Haggai urges the returned community and its leaders to rebuild the Temple and renew their commitment.

sources.title: Introduction to Haggai (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Zechariah
books.periodLabel: Persian-period restoration and Jerusalem's future
books.periodNote: Chapters 1–8 are associated with Temple restoration beginning in 520 BCE. Chapters 9–14 have later, disputed historical horizons; the collection is not confined to one brief ministry.
books.summary: Visions encourage the rebuilding community, while later oracles imagine kingship, conflict, purification and Jerusalem's future.

sources.title: Introduction to Zechariah (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Malachi
books.periodLabel: Postexilic Judah, probably the 5th century BCE
books.periodNote: A functioning Temple and Persian administration frame the disputes. The book's exact date is uncertain, including its relationship to the reforms associated with Nehemiah.
books.summary: Disputes over worship, fidelity and justice challenge priests and people, while promising judgment and a coming messenger.

sources.title: Introduction to Malachi (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Matthew
books.periodLabel: Jesus' birth to resurrection, around the turn of the era–30s CE
books.periodNote: The story begins in Herod's reign and ends with Jesus' death and resurrection. These narrative settings precede the Gospel's later first-century composition; precise dates remain approximate.
books.summary: Jesus teaches and heals in Galilee, travels to Jerusalem, is crucified, and commissions his followers after the resurrection.

sources.title: Introduction to Matthew (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

sources.title: The Chronology of the Life of Jesus (NLT Study Bible, pp. 1565–1566)

books.title: Mark
books.periodLabel: Jesus' public ministry, approximately the 20s–30s CE
books.periodNote: The account begins with John the Baptist and Jesus' adult ministry. Its narrative setting is earlier than the Gospel's composition in the first century.
books.summary: Jesus announces God's kingdom, heals and teaches, journeys to Jerusalem, and suffers death; women then find the tomb empty.

sources.title: Introduction to Mark (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

sources.title: The Chronology of the Life of Jesus (NLT Study Bible, pp. 1565–1566)

books.title: Luke
books.periodLabel: Jesus' birth to ascension, around the turn of the era–30s CE
books.periodNote: The infancy and ministry narratives belong to the early Roman imperial period. Their chronology requires care; Luke's Gospel was written later than the events it recounts.
books.summary: The stories of John and Jesus' births lead into Jesus' ministry, journey to Jerusalem, death, resurrection and ascension.

sources.title: Introduction to Luke (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

sources.title: The Chronology of the Life of Jesus (NLT Study Bible, pp. 1565–1566)

books.title: John
books.periodLabel: Jesus' public ministry, approximately the 20s–30s CE
books.periodNote: The prologue reaches back to creation; the main narrative concerns Jesus in early Roman Judaea and Galilee. Its setting is distinct from the Gospel's later first-century formation.
books.summary: Signs and extended conversations reveal Jesus' identity, leading to his final teaching, crucifixion, resurrection and appearances to disciples.

sources.title: Introduction to John (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

sources.title: The Chronology of the Life of Jesus (NLT Study Bible, pp. 1565–1566)

books.title: Acts
books.periodLabel: Apostolic missions, approximately the 30s–early 60s CE
books.periodNote: The narrative runs from Jesus' ascension to Paul's confinement in Rome. This is the period narrated, not a date for the book's composition.
books.summary: The movement spreads from Jerusalem through the eastern Mediterranean as Peter, Paul and other witnesses encounter new communities and opposition.

sources.title: Introduction to Acts (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Romans
books.periodLabel: Paul and the Roman churches, approximately the 50s CE
books.periodNote: The letter addresses communities during Paul's missionary work, usually dated 56–58 CE. Its discussion of Israel's past and future is not a continuous historical span.
books.summary: Paul develops his account of the gospel, faith, Israel and the nations, and the shared life of believers.

sources.title: Introduction to Romans (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 1 Corinthians
books.periodLabel: The Corinthian church, mid-50s CE
books.periodNote: This letter responds to particular questions and conflicts in a young community. Its historical setting is correspondence during Paul's ministry, not a narrated period of history.
books.summary: Paul addresses divisions, sexual ethics, worship, spiritual gifts, resurrection and practical responsibilities within the church.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Corinthians (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 2 Corinthians
books.periodLabel: Paul and Corinth, mid-to-late 50s CE
books.periodNote: The material is generally situated around 57 CE. Scholars debate whether the book combines several letters, so its contents may reflect more than one occasion.
books.summary: Paul seeks reconciliation, explains his ministry and sufferings, defends his authority, and urges support for the Jerusalem collection.

sources.title: Introduction to 2 Corinthians (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Galatians
books.periodLabel: Galatian churches, late 40s–50s CE
books.periodNote: The date depends partly on which Galatian communities are intended and how Paul's journeys are reconstructed. The letter addresses a contemporary dispute rather than a historical survey.
books.summary: Paul argues for Gentile inclusion apart from circumcision, recounts his calling, and describes freedom and life in the Spirit.

sources.title: Introduction to Galatians (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Ephesians
books.periodLabel: Early churches in Paul's tradition, 1st century CE
books.periodNote: The letter presents Paul as imprisoned. Pauline authorship and the date are debated; proposals include his lifetime and later first-century composition.
books.summary: The church is portrayed as united in Christ across Jewish and Gentile divisions, with that unity expressed in daily conduct.

sources.title: Introduction to Ephesians (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Philippians
books.periodLabel: Paul's imprisonment and the Philippian church, 50s–60s CE
books.periodNote: The place of imprisonment is uncertain, with Ephesus, Caesarea and Rome proposed. This range describes possible settings for the letter, not years of narrated events.
books.summary: Paul thanks the Philippians, urges unity and humility, reflects on Christ, and encourages steadfastness amid difficulty.

sources.title: Introduction to Philippians (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Colossians
books.periodLabel: The church at Colossae, 1st century CE
books.periodNote: The letter is presented as written from imprisonment. Its precise date and Pauline authorship are debated, so the community setting is more secure than a single year.
books.summary: Christ's cosmic importance grounds warnings against rival teachings and instructions for the community's renewed way of life.

sources.title: Introduction to Colossians (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 1 Thessalonians
books.periodLabel: The new Thessalonian church, around 50–51 CE
books.periodNote: This early letter belongs to Paul's missionary relationship with Thessalonica. Recollections of his visit and hopes for Christ's return do not form a continuous historical timeline.
books.summary: Paul reassures and instructs the community about faithfulness, holiness, mutual care and believers who have died.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Thessalonians (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 2 Thessalonians
books.periodLabel: The Thessalonian church in the Pauline tradition
books.periodNote: The letter addresses a community associated with Paul's mission. Its authorship and date are disputed; the portrayed apostolic setting should be distinguished from proposals for later composition.
books.summary: The community is encouraged under pressure and instructed about Christ's return, misleading claims and responsibility for work.

sources.title: New Testament Letters (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

sources.title: 2 Thessalonians 1–3 (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 1 Timothy
books.periodLabel: Church leadership in Paul's later-life setting
books.periodNote: The letter presents instructions from Paul to Timothy. The Pastoral Letters' authorship and composition dates are debated; their portrayed setting is not an independently fixed writing date.
books.summary: Timothy receives guidance about teaching, worship, leadership, care for community members and the use of wealth.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Timothy (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 2 Timothy
books.periodLabel: Paul's final imprisonment and farewell setting
books.periodNote: Paul is portrayed as a prisoner in Rome facing death. This literary setting is distinct from the debated authorship and composition of the Pastoral Letters.
books.summary: Timothy is urged to remain faithful, endure hardship, guard sound teaching and continue the work entrusted to him.

sources.title: Introduction to 2 Timothy (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Timothy (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Titus
books.periodLabel: The organization of churches on Crete
books.periodNote: The letter presents Paul instructing Titus during his ministry. Its composition and authorship are debated alongside the other Pastoral Letters; the setting does not establish an exact date.
books.summary: Titus receives instructions on appointing leaders, resisting disruptive teaching and encouraging conduct suited to the community's faith.

sources.title: Introduction to Titus (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Timothy (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Philemon
books.periodLabel: Paul's imprisonment, approximately the 50s–60s CE
books.periodNote: The letter's prison location and precise date are uncertain. Its setting is a personal appeal within Paul's network, rather than an extended historical narrative.
books.summary: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus, an enslaved man, in the transformed relationship of a beloved brother.

sources.title: Introduction to Philemon (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: Hebrews
books.periodLabel: An early Christian community, 1st century CE
books.periodNote: The author and precise date are unknown. Israel's wilderness sanctuary supplies the argument's imagery; it is not the historical setting of the audience.
books.summary: An extended exhortation presents Jesus as high priest and urges perseverance through scriptural interpretation, warnings and examples of faith.

sources.title: Introduction to Hebrews (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: James
books.periodLabel: Early Jewish-Christian communities
books.periodNote: The letter addresses a dispersed community in general terms. Its authorship and precise date are debated, and its teachings do not narrate one sequence of historical events.
books.summary: Practical instruction connects faith with action, addressing wisdom, speech, partiality, wealth, endurance and care for others.

sources.title: Introduction to James (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 1 Peter
books.periodLabel: Christian communities in Roman Asia Minor
books.periodNote: The letter names communities in several provinces and presents a Petrine voice. Authorship and first-century dating remain debated; the social pressure described need not imply an empire-wide persecution.
books.summary: Believers are encouraged to sustain hope, holiness and mutual care while responding faithfully to suffering and hostility.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 Peter (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 2 Peter
books.periodLabel: The apostolic farewell setting and later church generations
books.periodNote: The work presents Peter's farewell. Many scholars place its composition in the early second century, distinguishing that later setting from the apostolic voice it adopts.
books.summary: Warnings against false teachers accompany an appeal to inherited teaching, moral growth and confidence in Christ's promised return.

sources.title: Introduction to 2 Peter (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 1 John
books.periodLabel: Johannine communities, late 1st century CE
books.periodNote: The work addresses a community dispute and is commonly placed near the century's end. Its recollection of Jesus differs from the present setting of its audience.
books.summary: A theological exhortation links confession of Jesus with fellowship, love, obedience and discernment of competing claims.

sources.title: Introduction to 1 John (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 2 John
books.periodLabel: Johannine churches, late 1st century CE
books.periodNote: The precise place and date are unknown; a late first-century setting is plausible. The letter addresses a community through the image of a chosen lady and her children.
books.summary: The elder urges love and fidelity while warning against welcoming teachers who deny the confession of Christ.

sources.title: Introduction to 2 John (NABRE)
sources.institution: USCCB, New American Bible Revised Edition

books.title: 3 John
books.periodLabel: Johannine networks, late 1st century CE
books.periodNote: This personal letter belongs to the same broad network as 2 John. Its exact date and location remain uncertain; local relationships provide its immediate setting.

nodes.title: The Tel Dan Stele

discovery.label: Fragments excavated in 1993 and 1994.

nodes.dateBasis: Ninth-century attribution from inscription and historical context; the exact year is not fixed.
nodes.summary: A royal dynasty named in the Bible appears on a monument raised by a neighboring kingdom.
nodes.observation: Unearthed in fragments at Tel Dan in 1993 and 1994, this Aramaic inscription commemorates victories over the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. It is generally attributed to Hazael of Aram, although his name does not survive.
nodes.connection: The royal house associated with David in 2 Samuel has a counterpart in an independent, ninth-century BCE inscription. This is evidence for a recognized Davidic dynasty.
nodes.limit: It does not describe David’s life or establish the size of his kingdom. The monument is a later royal victory account; parts of its wording require reconstruction.

quotes.text: And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.
quotes.fullText: And thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee: thy throne shall be established for ever.
quotes.editorialNote: The dynastic promise supplies the comparison; the inscription is later evidence for a royal house, not a transcript of this promise.

nodes.title: The Silver Amulets

discovery.label: Excavated in 1979.

nodes.dateBasis: Late seventh to early sixth century BCE, based on archaeological context and letter forms. Numeric endpoints are approximate period brackets.
nodes.summary: Tiny silver scrolls preserve an early form of a blessing still read and spoken today.
nodes.observation: Two rolled silver amulets were discovered in a burial repository at Ketef Hinnom in 1979. A detailed 2004 reexamination supported a date near the end of the kingdom of Judah, before the Babylonian exile.
nodes.connection: Their protective language overlaps with the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24–26. They are among the earliest surviving witnesses to wording also preserved in the Hebrew Bible.
nodes.limit: The amulets are not manuscripts of Numbers. Shared wording may reflect a liturgical tradition; it does not date the composition or final form of the whole book. Their dating and reconstruction have also been discussed by scholars.

quotes.text: The LORD bless thee, and keep thee:
quotes.fullText: The LORD bless thee, and keep thee:
quotes.editorialNote: Biblical blessing parallel; the displayed KJV verse is not an exact translation of every surviving amulet letter.

nodes.title: The Great Isaiah Scroll

discovery.label: Recovered from Qumran Cave 1 in 1947.

nodes.dateBasis: Conventionally dated around 125 BCE. The numeric bracket is for orientation, not an exact copying date.
nodes.summary: An ancient copy of Isaiah brings the history of biblical transmission into view.
nodes.observation: The Great Isaiah Scroll, conventionally dated to around 125 BCE, was among the scrolls recovered from Qumran Cave 1 in 1947. It preserves all 66 chapters of Isaiah.
nodes.connection: As a surviving biblical manuscript, it provides direct evidence for an ancient form of Isaiah. Comparison with the later Masoretic tradition reveals substantial continuity alongside differences in spelling and wording.
nodes.limit: An ancient copy is not an author’s original. The evidence does not show that every letter remained unchanged, or settle when each part of Isaiah was composed.

quotes.text: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
quotes.fullText: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

nodes.title: Sennacherib’s Prism

discovery.label: Acquired in 1830; distinguish acquisition from a documented excavation date.

nodes.dateBasis: The Taylor Prism dates to 691 BCE and recounts the earlier campaign of 701 BCE.
nodes.summary: An Assyrian king tells his side of the campaign against Judah and King Hezekiah.
nodes.observation: The six-sided Taylor Prism, dated to 691 BCE, records Sennacherib’s campaigns. Acquired in 1830, it is one of several surviving prisms that preserve versions of his annals.
nodes.connection: Its account of the 701 BCE campaign names Hezekiah and Jerusalem. Second Kings 18–19 also describes the Assyrian invasion of Judah and Hezekiah’s tribute.
nodes.limit: Assyrian royal inscriptions celebrate the king’s achievements. The accounts differ in emphasis and details; the prism does not verify the biblical explanation for Jerusalem’s deliverance.

quotes.text: Now in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah did Sennacherib king of Assyria come up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them.
quotes.fullText: Now in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah did Sennacherib king of Assyria come up against all the fenced cities of Judah, and took them.

nodes.title: The Lachish Reliefs

discovery.label: Nineteenth-century excavations at Nineveh; exact recovery date not established in this record.

nodes.dateBasis: Museum date for the palace reliefs, after the campaign represented.
nodes.summary: A palace wall depicts the capture of a Judean city named in the biblical account.
nodes.observation: These reliefs decorated Sennacherib’s South-West Palace. They depict the Assyrian siege and capture of Lachish in 701 BCE, including soldiers, siege equipment, captives, and booty.
nodes.connection: Second Kings 18 places Sennacherib at Lachish during the invasion of Judah. The reliefs provide an Assyrian visual account of that city’s defeat.
nodes.limit: The reliefs are royal representations, composed to display Assyrian power. Their scenes should be read as selective storytelling, not as a neutral photographic record.

quotes.text: And the king of Assyria sent Tartan and Rabsaris and Rab-shakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a great host against Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem. And when they were come up, they came and stood by the…
quotes.fullText: And the king of Assyria sent Tartan and Rabsaris and Rab-shakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a great host against Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem. And when they were come up, they came and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, which is in the highway of the fuller’s field.

nodes.title: The Pilate Inscription

discovery.label: Discovered at Caesarea in 1961.

nodes.dateBasis: Dated to Pilate’s administration; the selected scholarly edition uses approximately 26–37 CE.
nodes.summary: A damaged dedication preserves the name and office of the Roman governor in the Gospels.
nodes.observation: Discovered at Caesarea in 1961, the damaged Latin dedication preserves portions of Pilate’s name and his title, reconstructed as prefect of Judaea. It dates to his first-century administration.
nodes.connection: Luke 3:1 names Pontius Pilate as governor of Judaea. The inscription supplies contemporary material evidence for that official and clarifies his formal Roman title.
nodes.limit: Parts of the inscription are restored by scholars. It does not mention Jesus or describe his trial, and the precise nature of the building named in the dedication remains debated.

quotes.text: Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Cæsar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judæa, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene,
quotes.fullText: Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Cæsar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judæa, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene,

nodes.title: Merneptah Stele
nodes.place: Thebes, Egypt; campaign refers to the southern Levant

discovery.label: Found by Flinders Petrie at Thebes in 1896

nodes.summary: An Egyptian victory inscription names Israel as a people in the southern Levant near the end of the Late Bronze Age.
nodes.observation: The inscription includes Israel among Merneptah's defeated enemies. Its Egyptian writing marks Israel as a people, unlike the city names nearby.
nodes.connection: This supplies an external chronological anchor for a people called Israel in Canaan, the setting of biblical settlement traditions. The selected passages provide context, not an inscription-to-verse match.
nodes.limit: A royal victory claim does not establish the Exodus, Joshua's campaigns, or Israel's origins. Its boast of destruction is not a population census.
nodes.dateBasis: Merneptah's victory inscription is conventionally dated 1208/1207 BCE. The stone had an earlier inscription; this date concerns Merneptah's text. It sits at the Late Bronze–Iron Age transition, grouped under iron here.

quotes.text: Now after the death of Joshua it came to pass, that the children of Israel asked the LORD, saying, Who shall go up for us against the Canaanites first, to fight against them?
quotes.fullText: Now after the death of Joshua it came to pass, that the children of Israel asked the LORD, saying, Who shall go up for us against the Canaanites first, to fight against them?
quotes.editorialNote: Names Israel in the land; this is contextual, not an identification of Merneptah's campaign with the narrated fighting.

quotes.text: And Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem, and called for the elders of Israel, and for their heads, and for their judges, and for their officers; and they presented themselves before God.
quotes.fullText: And Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem, and called for the elders of Israel, and for their heads, and for their judges, and for their officers; and they presented themselves before God.
quotes.editorialNote: Names Israel's tribes; the stele does not name Joshua or attest this assembly.

nodes.title: Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III
nodes.place: Kurkh, southeastern Turkey; account of Qarqar, Syria

discovery.label: Found by John George Taylor in October 1861; donated in 1863

nodes.summary: Shalmaneser III's campaign inscription identifies Ahab of Israel among the rulers opposing Assyria at Qarqar.
nodes.observation: The Akkadian inscription lists Ahab of Israel and forces attributed to him within an anti-Assyrian coalition. It belongs to Shalmaneser III's royal campaign record.
nodes.connection: It independently situates the Ahab known from Kings within ninth-century international politics. The battle of Qarqar itself is not narrated in the biblical passages.
nodes.limit: The reported troop totals and decisive Assyrian victory belong to royal self-presentation. Attesting Ahab does not establish every episode about him in Kings.
nodes.dateBasis: The text ends with Shalmaneser's sixth-year campaign at Qarqar in 853 BCE; erection is inferred around 853–852. CDLI identifies the object as BM 118884 and links its scholarly edition.

quotes.text: And in the thirty and eighth year of Asa king of Judah began Ahab the son of Omri to reign over Israel: and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty and two years.
quotes.fullText: And in the thirty and eighth year of Asa king of Judah began Ahab the son of Omri to reign over Israel: and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty and two years.
quotes.editorialNote: Names Ahab and Omri. Qarqar is not narrated in this verse or elsewhere in Kings.

nodes.title: Mesha Stele
nodes.place: Dhiban, ancient Dibon, Moab; present-day Jordan

discovery.label: Reported by Frederick Augustus Klein in 1868; broken and subsequently reconstructed

nodes.summary: Mesha's Moabite monument presents his recovery of territory from Israel, offering another political and religious perspective on conflict remembered in Kings.
nodes.observation: Thirty-four lines of Moabite writing on a restored basalt monument celebrate Mesha's victories over Israel and credit the Moabite god Chemosh.
nodes.connection: Kings also names Mesha, king of Moab, and describes rebellion against Israel. The two accounts create a useful comparison of named rulers, territory, and competing interpretations.
nodes.limit: The accounts differ in perspective and detail; neither should silently be rewritten to match the other. The monument is fragmentary, with restoration dependent partly on an early paper impression.
nodes.dateBasis: The Louvre catalog assigns 830–805 BCE but its descriptive text says shortly after 842. The broad ninth-century label preserves that inconsistency instead of presenting a single secure year.

quotes.text: And Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool.
quotes.fullText: And Mesha king of Moab was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel an hundred thousand lambs, and an hundred thousand rams, with the wool.

nodes.title: Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III
nodes.place: Nimrud, ancient Kalhu, Assyria; present-day Iraq

discovery.label: Excavated by Austen Henry Layard at Nimrud in 1846

eventDate.label: Tribute associated with Jehu, c. 841 BCE

nodes.summary: An Assyrian monument names tribute from Jehu of Israel and illustrates a submitting delegation, providing a contemporary external setting for his reign.
nodes.observation: A caption identifies tribute from Jehu, associated with the house of Omri. The relief includes a prostrating figure within a sequence of foreign tribute scenes.
nodes.connection: Jehu also appears in Kings. The monument places his kingdom within Assyria's tributary network, an episode not explicitly narrated in those chapters.
nodes.limit: The scene does not establish that Jehu personally visited Assyria or preserve a portrait from life. The monument celebrates Assyrian power.
nodes.dateBasis: The monument was erected in 825 BCE; the Jehu tribute episode belongs around 841 BCE. These are distinct timeline dates.

quotes.text: And the time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty and eight years.
quotes.fullText: And the time that Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty and eight years.

nodes.title: Siloam Tunnel Inscription

discovery.label: Found inside the water tunnel in Jerusalem in 1880

nodes.summary: An ancient Hebrew inscription describes tunnel crews meeting underground, preserving a local account of Jerusalem's water engineering.
nodes.observation: The text recounts the breakthrough between opposing work crews and water reaching the pool. It names neither a king nor an absolute year.
nodes.connection: The tunnel is commonly associated with Hezekiah's waterworks described in Kings and Chronicles. That historical identification is an inference from archaeological and textual context.
nodes.limit: The inscription does not itself name Hezekiah or Sennacherib. Identifying the project with preparations for 701 BCE requires evidence beyond its words.
nodes.dateBasis: A recent Jerusalem inscription corpus assigns late eighth–early seventh century BCE. Numeric endpoints are broad half-century plotting bounds, not measured limits; the inscription has no explicit calendar date.

quotes.text: And the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made a pool, and a conduit, and brought water into the city, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
quotes.fullText: And the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made a pool, and a conduit, and brought water into the city, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?

quotes.text: This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.
quotes.fullText: This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.

nodes.title: Lachish Letters, especially Letter 4

discovery.label: First group excavated in 1935; additional letters found in 1938

nodes.summary: Hebrew messages on pottery preserve military communication in Judah; Letter 4 links watching Lachish's signals with an inability to see Azekah.
nodes.observation: Letter 4 discusses signal watching between fortified locations. The letters give direct evidence of written correspondence and military administration in Judah near the end of the monarchy.
nodes.connection: Jeremiah also names Lachish and Azekah among Judah's remaining fortified cities and mentions warning signals. The letters illuminate that historical setting and communication practice.
nodes.limit: Not seeing Azekah need not mean it had already fallen: visibility and relay arrangements offer another explanation. The letters are not copies of Jeremiah or proof of each narrated event.
nodes.dateBasis: Early sixth-century context before Lachish's Babylonian destruction; some individual letters are conventionally dated 589–587 BCE. The broader range avoids assigning every letter to one siege day.

quotes.text: When the king of Babylon’s army fought against Jerusalem, and against all the cities of Judah that were left, against Lachish, and against Azekah: for these defenced cities remained of the cities of Judah.
quotes.fullText: When the king of Babylon’s army fought against Jerusalem, and against all the cities of Judah that were left, against Lachish, and against Azekah: for these defenced cities remained of the cities of Judah.

nodes.title: Babylonian Chronicle: Capture of Jerusalem
nodes.dateLabel: Tablet-copy date unresolved; event in 597 BCE
nodes.place: Babylonia; exact archaeological findspot unrecorded in the consulted catalog

discovery.label: Discovery circumstances unrecorded in the consulted CDLI catalog

nodes.summary: BM 21946 records Nebuchadnezzar's capture of the city of Judah and replacement of its king, providing a dated external counterpart to Jerusalem's surrender.
nodes.observation: The chronicle dates the capture to Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year, in Addaru. It describes taking the king and appointing a replacement but does not name either Judean ruler.
nodes.connection: Read alongside Kings, the episode aligns with the surrender involving Jehoiachin and Zedekiah in 597 BCE. Identification of the unnamed rulers comes from comparing sources.
nodes.limit: The tablet does not narrate the later destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BCE. Regnal-year numbering differs between relevant biblical passages and requires explanation rather than silent harmonization.
nodes.dateBasis: 597 BCE dates the narrated capture, not the surviving tablet's manufacture. CDLI supplies only a broad Neo-Babylonian period classification; a more precise copy date remains unverified here.

quotes.text: And Jehoiachin the king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon, he, and his mother, and his servants, and his princes, and his officers: and the king of Babylon took him in the eighth year of his reign.
quotes.fullText: And Jehoiachin the king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon, he, and his mother, and his servants, and his princes, and his officers: and the king of Babylon took him in the eighth year of his reign.
quotes.editorialNote: Kings uses an eighth regnal year; the chronicle uses a seventh. Preserve the distinction in the detail page.

quotes.text: This is the people whom Nebuchadrezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year three thousand Jews and three and twenty:
quotes.fullText: This is the people whom Nebuchadrezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year three thousand Jews and three and twenty:

nodes.title: Jehoiachin ration tablets
nodes.dateLabel: c. 592 BCE; related tablets 6th century BCE

discovery.label: Excavated at Babylon; the selected museum record does not specify a discovery year

nodes.summary: Babylonian administrative records name Jehoiachin and Judean royal dependents among recipients of provisions.
nodes.observation: Oil-ration lists from Nebuchadnezzar II’s court include Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and members of his household. Berlin catalogs one fragment as VAT 16378.
nodes.connection: The records independently place the Judean king in Babylon, matching the setting of his exile in Kings and Jeremiah.
nodes.limit: The dated ration evidence precedes the release under Nebuchadnezzar’s successor narrated in 2 Kings 25. It does not document that later release or establish continuous imprisonment.
nodes.dateBasis: The Posen Library dates its translated ration texts to 592 BCE; Berlin’s VAT 16378 record gives the broader sixth century BCE. The group should not be treated as one exactly dated tablet.

quotes.text: And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life.
quotes.fullText: And his allowance was a continual allowance given him of the king, a daily rate for every day, all the days of his life.
quotes.editorialNote: This verse concerns a later royal allowance; the tablets do not establish the date of Jehoiachin's release.

quotes.text: And for his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
quotes.fullText: And for his diet, there was a continual diet given him of the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.
quotes.editorialNote: This verse concerns a later allowance than the selected ration tablets.

nodes.title: The Cyrus Cylinder

discovery.label: Excavated at Babylon in 1879

nodes.summary: Cyrus’s Babylonian royal inscription describes conquest, religious restoration, and the return of displaced communities.
nodes.observation: The cylinder presents Cyrus’s capture of Babylon and his restoration of divine images and sanctuaries, with people returned to their homelands.
nodes.connection: Its imperial setting offers context for biblical traditions about Cyrus, including the return and rebuilding decree in Ezra.
nodes.limit: The cylinder does not name Jews or Jerusalem. It is not the decree quoted in Ezra and cannot independently establish that decree’s wording or specific implementation.
nodes.dateBasis: Inscribed after Cyrus captured Babylon in 539 BCE; the museum’s hosted object entry uses 539 BCE. This is the approximate inscription date, not the excavation date.

quotes.text: Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The LORD God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah.
quotes.fullText: Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The LORD God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him an house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah.
quotes.editorialNote: The cylinder offers context for royal restoration policy; it does not mention Jerusalem or reproduce this decree.

quotes.text: That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid.
quotes.fullText: That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid.

nodes.title: Elephantine festival letter

discovery.label: Berlin expedition, 1906–1907

nodes.summary: An Aramaic letter to a Judean community in Egypt preserves instructions connected with the festival of Unleavened Bread.
nodes.observation: Papyrus P 13464 is a damaged letter from Hananiah to Jedaniah and the Jewish garrison. It discusses festival dates and observance under Persian rule.
nodes.connection: Its instructions belong to the same ritual world as biblical laws about Unleavened Bread, providing evidence for festival practice in a diaspora community.
nodes.limit: The familiar title ‘Passover letter’ includes interpretation: the word Passover is not preserved in the surviving fragments. The letter does not establish the final form of the Torah.
nodes.dateBasis: Berlin’s catalog gives 419 BCE; its exhibition documentation gives 419–418 BCE. The wider range preserves this calendrical uncertainty.

quotes.text: Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; even the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses: for whosoever eateth leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel.
quotes.fullText: Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; even the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses: for whosoever eateth leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel.

quotes.text: And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread unto the LORD: seven days ye must eat unleavened bread.
quotes.fullText: And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread unto the LORD: seven days ye must eat unleavened bread.

quotes.text: And in the fifteenth day of this month is the feast: seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten.
quotes.fullText: And in the fifteenth day of this month is the feast: seven days shall unleavened bread be eaten.

nodes.title: The Gallio inscription

discovery.label: Fragments recovered between 1885 and 1910

nodes.summary: An inscribed imperial letter names Gallio as proconsul, offering an external chronological anchor for the setting of Acts 18.
nodes.observation: Fragments of a Greek letter of Claudius to Delphi mention Junius Gallio and his proconsular office. Imperial titles provide the dating framework.
nodes.connection: Acts places Paul before Gallio in Achaia. The inscription helps constrain the official’s tenure and, when combined with Acts, the possible chronology of Paul’s stay.
nodes.limit: The inscription does not mention Paul or the hearing. Reconstruction supplies missing letters, and translating the imperial date into the exact limits of Gallio’s tenure requires inference.
nodes.dateBasis: Claudius’s regnal and imperial titles place the letter around 52 CE. This dates the letter; it is not a direct date for the hearing in Acts.

quotes.text: And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat,
quotes.fullText: And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat,

nodes.title: The Erastus pavement

discovery.label: Inscribed slabs found in 1928–1929; additional recovery later

nodes.summary: A Corinthian pavement names an Erastus who funded civic paving; identification with Paul’s associate remains disputed.
nodes.observation: The Latin inscription records an Erastus paying for paving in connection with his aedileship. The personal name survives, but the complete Roman name does not.
nodes.connection: Romans 16:23 mentions an Erastus with a civic financial role. The shared name and city invite comparison, while the offices and date complicate identification.
nodes.limit: Both the pavement’s date and the identification are contested. It should not be counted as a confirmed independent attestation of Paul’s Erastus.
nodes.dateBasis: Kent’s excavation publication places it near the mid-first century; Friesen argues for the mid-second. The displayed interval brackets competing proposals, not a continuously probable range.

quotes.text: Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother.
quotes.fullText: Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you. Erastus the chamberlain of the city saluteth you, and Quartus a brother.
quotes.editorialNote: The identification of this Erastus with the pavement donor is disputed; the offices must not be silently equated.

quotes.text: Erastus abode at Corinth: but Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick.
quotes.fullText: Erastus abode at Corinth: but Trophimus have I left at Miletum sick.
quotes.editorialNote: This names Erastus in Corinth but does not establish that he is the pavement donor.

nodes.title: The Bethesda pool complex
nodes.dateLabel: Early Roman phase; late 1st century BCE–1st century CE

discovery.label: Excavations began in 1862; pool recorded in 1873; work continued into the 20th century

nodes.summary: Excavated twin pools near St Anne’s illuminate the physical setting of John’s Bethesda narrative.
nodes.observation: Excavations revealed two large pools divided by a barrier wall, with later Roman, Byzantine, and medieval structures. Structural analysis distinguishes successive phases.
nodes.connection: The double-pool layout provides a plausible setting for John 5. Its association with five porticoes also draws on ancient descriptions and architectural reconstruction.
nodes.limit: The physical setting does not establish the healing narrative. Surviving columns cannot simply be labeled John’s porticoes; the site’s phases and functions require archaeological interpretation.
nodes.dateBasis: Gibson identifies an Early Roman structural phase, beginning in the Herodian period. The numerical interval is a period bracket for orientation, not a measured construction date.

quotes.text: Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches.

nodes.summary: A small codex fragment preserves part of John’s account of Jesus before Pilate.
nodes.observation: Greek writing on both sides preserves portions of John 18. Manchester’s catalog notes the original 100–150 CE estimate and later research suggesting nearer 200 CE.

nodes.title: En-Gedi Leviticus Scroll

discovery.label: Excavated in 1970; digitally read in work published in 2016.

nodes.summary: Virtual unwrapping recovered Leviticus text from a charred synagogue scroll.
nodes.observation: Imaging revealed portions of two columns. The 2016 study reports agreement between the recovered consonantal text and the medieval Masoretic text.
nodes.connection: This is a later material witness to Leviticus, which belongs to the Bible’s wilderness narrative. The manuscript’s survival illuminates textual transmission.
nodes.limit: The result concerns the deciphered text, not the entire Bible. Radiocarbon analysis favors the third or fourth century CE; a palaeographic proposal places it earlier.
nodes.dateBasis: Radiocarbon results reported in Seales et al. (2016); the same paper notes Yardeni’s first- or second-century palaeographic alternative.

nodes.title: A Mari letter about finding pasture
nodes.summary: A report describes households moving with their flocks because pasture is unavailable.

nodes.title: Deir ‘Alla · Balaam son of Beor

discovery.label: Painted plaster fragments excavated in March 1967.

nodes.summary: A painted plaster text names Balaam son of Beor, the seer also named in Numbers.
nodes.observation: Red and black writing on plaster preserves a narrative about a seer named Balaam son of Beor and his divine vision.
nodes.connection: The matching name and patronymic establish an extra-biblical Balaam tradition in the region. The inscription tells a different story from Numbers.
nodes.limit: This is evidence for the circulation of the figure and tradition, not contemporary documentation of Balaam’s journey or the speaking donkey. Reading and reconstruction remain debated.
nodes.dateBasis: The BAS scholarly discussion places the inscription and archaeological context around 800 BCE. Some scholarship uses a later date; the numeric bracket is approximate.

nodes.title: Al-Yahudu · Judean families in Babylonia
nodes.dateLabel: 572–477 BCE in the selected published corpus

discovery.label: Surfaced on the antiquities market; not recovered in a documented scientific excavation.

nodes.summary: Dated legal tablets record Judean households living and working in Babylonia.
nodes.observation: Documents from Al-Yahudu and nearby settlements preserve names, transactions, agricultural obligations, and family connections across generations.
nodes.connection: They provide an external documentary view of Judean life in exile and the continuing diaspora described in biblical literature.
nodes.limit: They do not identify Jeremiah, Ezekiel, or Daniel. Missing excavation context limits reconstruction of the archive; individual transactions are not a full census of the exiles.
nodes.dateBasis: Internal Babylonian dates place the selected corpus between 572 and 477 BCE; this is a corpus span, not the date of one tablet.

nodes.title: Bisotun · Darius’s account of his accession

discovery.label: A surviving rock monument; no single modern discovery date assigned.

nodes.summary: Darius I set his account of royal accession and rebellions into a three-language rock inscription.
nodes.observation: The monument combines a royal relief with inscriptions in Elamite, Babylonian, and Old Persian describing Darius’s establishment of power.
nodes.connection: It independently documents the Persian ruler whose reign supplies the setting for rebuilding in Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah.
nodes.limit: The inscription is Darius’s own political account and does not reproduce Ezra’s temple decree. Darius I should not be equated automatically with Daniel’s Darius the Mede.
nodes.dateBasis: UNESCO’s monument description associates its creation with Darius’s accession and campaigns of 521–520 BCE; different textual phases exist.

nodes.title: Elephantine’s petition to rebuild its temple

discovery.label: Excavated by the Royal Museums’ expedition in the early twentieth century.

nodes.summary: An Aramaic petition asks the governor of Judea for help rebuilding a temple of YHW in Egypt.
nodes.observation: Berlin papyrus P 13495 preserves an appeal by the Elephantine community after the destruction of its temple. The catalog connects the appeal with Bagohi and the sons of Sanballat.
nodes.connection: The document links a Jewish community in Egypt with Persian-period Judean and Samarian administration. It supplies context for the world of Ezra–Nehemiah and a comparison with Isaiah’s Egyptian altar passage.
nodes.limit: The temple is not thereby established as the fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecy. Identifications of named officials must be checked individually against chronology and editions.
nodes.dateBasis: The museum dates the papyrus to 25 November 407 BCE in the reign of Darius II.

nodes.title: Nabonidus Chronicle · the fall of Babylon

nodes.summary: A Babylonian chronicle records Nabonidus’s absence and the Persian takeover of Babylon.
nodes.observation: The tablet’s annalistic account describes Nabonidus’s reign and the entry of Cyrus’s forces into Babylon in 539 BCE.
nodes.connection: It gives an external chronological framework for the end of Babylonian rule and the beginning of the Persian period reflected in Daniel and Ezra.
nodes.limit: The chronicle does not narrate Daniel’s banquet or the writing on the wall. Its surviving copy is later than the events it records, and its perspective must be assessed alongside other texts.
nodes.dateBasis: The British Museum’s catalog presentation dates the object to 299–100 BCE while its historical contents concern Nabonidus and Cyrus in the sixth century BCE.

nodes.title: Shoshenq I's Karnak campaign list
nodes.summary: A pharaoh's monumental list records claimed victories in the southern Levant during the period of the divided kingdoms.
nodes.observation: The portal preserves Shoshenq I's victory scenes and town or people names enclosed in captive-shaped rings.
nodes.connection: Shoshenq I is commonly identified with the Shishak of Kings and Chronicles. His campaign supplies an Egyptian counterpart to the biblical account of Egyptian intervention.
nodes.limit: A damaged royal conquest list is selective propaganda. Matching the ruler does not demonstrate every detail of the biblical raid or the fate of Jerusalem's treasures.
nodes.dateBasis: Digital Karnak dates construction within Shoshenq I's reign, 945–924 BCE. Those are reign bounds, not an exact date for every campaign or carving.

nodes.title: Sargon II's Samaria conquest account
nodes.status: Royal claim; chronology and figures require comparison
nodes.summary: Sargon's display inscription claims Samaria's conquest, deportations, and the installation of Assyrian administration.
nodes.observation: RINAP 2 text 7 describes captives from Samaria, chariot recruitment, an appointed governor, and imposed tribute. Surviving witnesses differ in the deportation total.
nodes.connection: Kings likewise describes Samaria's fall, deportation, and population transfers. Sargon's account gives an Assyrian perspective on the northern kingdom's absorption.
nodes.limit: The relationship between Shalmaneser V's siege and Sargon's claims needs historical reconstruction. Variant totals should not be presented as an independently audited census.
nodes.dateBasis: Broad production bracket within Sargon's reign; this does not assign the inscription's manufacture to the year of Samaria's fall.

nodes.title: Tiglath-pileser III on Pekah and Hoshea
nodes.summary: A fragmentary Assyrian summary inscription names Pekah and Hoshea during Israel's change of rulers.
nodes.observation: The text refers to the House of Omri, Pekah's removal, Hoshea's appointment, and wealth carried to Assyria.
nodes.connection: Kings names the same succession and describes Assyrian pressure. The inscription presents Hoshea's kingship as dependent on the Assyrian monarch.
nodes.limit: The damaged verb allows different readings of responsibility for Pekah's death. Assyrian sponsorship and the coup described in Kings are distinct claims to compare.
nodes.dateBasis: The accessible edition supplies the king's reign bracket. No narrower manufacture date or modern recovery year is asserted.

nodes.title: Esarhaddon's prism naming Manasseh
nodes.summary: Manasseh of Judah appears among the western rulers mobilized for Esarhaddon's building program.
nodes.observation: The prism lists Manasseh with other vassal kings whose resources supported work at Nineveh.
nodes.connection: It independently attests a Judahite king named Manasseh and places his reign within Assyria's imperial network.
nodes.limit: This building account does not describe Manasseh's imprisonment or repentance in Chronicles. Vassal service alone cannot verify those episodes.
nodes.dateBasis: The selected edition assigns the Nineveh prism to 673–672 BCE.

nodes.observation: BM 114789 records gold belonging to Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, titled rab sha reshi, sent to the Esangila temple.
nodes.connection: The combination of name, office, and period supports identification with Nebo-Sarsekim in Jeremiah 39:3; segmentation of the Hebrew names also matters.
nodes.limit: A probable identification is not certainty. The receipt concerns a temple payment and does not describe Jerusalem's siege or the official's presence there.
nodes.dateBasis: Tablet dated day 18 of Shabatu in Nebuchadnezzar's tenth year. The cited publication gives 595 BCE; the broader 595/594 bracket avoids silently resolving calendar conversion differences.

discovery.label: Recovered during the 2005 Zeitah excavation season.

nodes.title: Tel Zayit alphabet inscription
nodes.summary: An alphabet inscribed on a reused stone documents writing in the southern Levant during the early monarchy's conventional period.
nodes.observation: The excavators identified a 22-letter alphabet in two lines on a stone incorporated into a building wall.
nodes.connection: The find helps investigate the scribal setting implied by references to royal secretaries. That is a contextual connection, not a record of David or Solomon.
nodes.limit: Alphabet knowledge does not prove the composition of a biblical book or the scale of a kingdom. The script's cultural classification and broader implications remain debated.
nodes.dateBasis: Primary publication assigns the archaeological context to the tenth century BCE; this is an excavator attribution rather than an inscribed year.

nodes.title: Gezer agricultural calendar
nodes.summary: A short agricultural schedule records seasonal work, providing local context for the farming cycles underlying biblical festivals.
nodes.observation: The tablet lists activities such as sowing, flax cutting, and grain and fruit harvests, grouped into months or pairs of months.
nodes.connection: Its agricultural rhythm can be compared with harvest festivals in Exodus and Deuteronomy. It also witnesses early alphabetic writing.
nodes.limit: It does not quote festival laws or establish their date. A school exercise is one proposed function; identifying the language specifically as Hebrew is uncertain.
nodes.dateBasis: The selected edition uses a conventional tenth-century palaeographic attribution; the find came from excavation debris rather than a securely sealed context.

nodes.title: Samaria's wine and oil records
nodes.status: Administrative evidence; purpose and literacy debated
nodes.summary: Ink inscriptions on pottery record wine and oil deliveries to Israel's capital.
nodes.observation: The receipts preserve personal names, localities, commodities, and regnal-year formulas. Modern handwriting analysis identifies a small number of scribes within the studied sample.
nodes.connection: They reveal the economic and scribal setting of northern Israel, the kingdom addressed by Amos. They are documentary evidence from the society itself.
nodes.limit: The texts do not name the reigning king. Their exact administrative purpose and what a limited scribal sample says about general literacy require interpretation.
nodes.dateBasis: The selected study places the assemblage in the first half of the eighth century BCE; regnal years alone do not identify a particular reign.

nodes.title: Arad military correspondence
nodes.summary: Orders and accounts on potsherds document Judah's provisioning and military communications near the monarchy's end.
nodes.observation: The corpus includes food and wine allocations, troop-related orders, personal correspondence, and references to Judah's king and the house of YHWH.
nodes.connection: It supplies a material setting for written administration and scribal activity in late Judah, relevant to the world depicted in Kings and Jeremiah.
nodes.limit: Identifying several writers supports a literate administration; it does not date the authorship or final editing of a particular biblical book.
nodes.dateBasis: The principal military assemblage is dated around 600 BCE; numeric endpoints indicate approximation, not the duration of every text's use.

nodes.title: Arad shrine and altar residues
nodes.status: Excavated cult practice; biblical comparison contextual
nodes.summary: A Judahite shrine's altars preserve residues of incense ingredients, allowing ritual practice to be studied through laboratory analysis.
nodes.observation: Researchers detected compounds associated with cannabis on one altar and frankincense on another, along with substances interpreted as burning aids.
nodes.connection: The findings illuminate local incense use in Judah and invite comparison with biblical incense prescriptions and accounts of cult reform.
nodes.limit: Residues from Arad do not establish the recipe used at Jerusalem or explain a biblical term for incense. Attribution of shrine closure to a named reform remains a separate question.
nodes.dateBasis: The residue study identifies the altars with the eighth-century Judahite shrine. It does not directly date each burning episode.

nodes.title: Kuntillet Ajrud blessing inscriptions
nodes.summary: Blessings mentioning YHWH of Samaria and YHWH of Teman provide evidence for religious language beyond the biblical manuscripts.
nodes.observation: Inscriptions on pottery and plaster pair forms of YHWH's name with the expression commonly translated as his asherah.
nodes.connection: These writings provide context for biblical disputes about worship and Asherah. They show religious expression associated with Israel outside Jerusalem.
nodes.limit: The meaning of asherah and its relationship to adjacent drawings require interpretation. The inscriptions should not be treated as straightforward illustrations of an entire biblical theology.
nodes.dateBasis: The excavation publication places the site around 800 BCE. Numeric endpoints are approximate orientation brackets.

nodes.title: Excavated seal impression of Hezekiah
nodes.summary: A clay sealing bears Hezekiah's name, patronymic, and title as king of Judah.
nodes.observation: The excavated impression identifies Hezekiah as son of Ahaz and king of Judah, alongside a winged sun and ankh signs.
nodes.connection: The name, father, and royal title align with the ruler in Kings and Isaiah. Excavated context strengthens its evidential value compared with unprovenanced market pieces.
nodes.limit: The sealing came from refuse rather than an intact archive. Its imagery does not establish the king's personal beliefs, medical history, or every event associated with his reign.
nodes.dateBasis: The university announcement uses 727–698 BCE for Hezekiah's reign; the refuse context was assigned to his time or shortly afterward. This is not a calendar date stamped on the object.
