nodes.title: Silwan royal-steward tomb inscription
nodes.status: Office attested; identification with Shebna uncertain
nodes.summary: A tomb inscription identifies a royal steward, but its damaged personal name prevents a certain identification with Isaiah's Shebna.
nodes.observation: The surviving text names an official's position, identifies a burial, denies that treasure is inside, and warns against disturbing it.
nodes.connection: Isaiah criticizes the royal steward Shebna for preparing an elaborate tomb. That passage underlies a proposed restoration of this inscription's missing name.
nodes.limit: Using Isaiah to restore a damaged name and then treating the restored name as independent proof would be circular. The office and burial practice are firmer evidence.
nodes.dateBasis: The selected edition dates the inscription approximately to 700 BCE; numeric endpoints are only a broad orientation bracket.

quotes.text: Thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say, What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as…
quotes.fullText: Thus saith the Lord GOD of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house, and say, What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, as he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, and that graveth an habitation for himself in a rock?
quotes.editorialNote: These verses name Shebna, his office, and his tomb; restoring the damaged inscription from this text does not independently establish the identity.

nodes.title: LMLK royal storage-jar stamps
nodes.summary: Stamped jar handles marked as belonging to the king reveal an organized system of storage and distribution in Judah.
nodes.observation: The stamps combine the royal designation with symbols and words including Hebron, Ziph, and Socoh. They occur widely across Judah.
nodes.connection: They provide material evidence for royal administration and stored agricultural products in the period of Hezekiah and Assyrian pressure.
nodes.limit: The exact fiscal system, the reading of MMST, and how directly production relates to military preparations remain debated. The stamps do not name Hezekiah.
nodes.dateBasis: The selected study assigns this stamp tradition to the late eighth century BCE and reviews competing explanations of its development.

nodes.title: Jerusalem's Broad Wall
nodes.summary: A massive fortification demonstrates that Iron Age Jerusalem extended onto the Western Hill.
nodes.observation: Excavation exposed a substantial city wall and earlier domestic remains along its route, supplying physical evidence of urban expansion and defensive construction.
nodes.connection: The wall is commonly discussed alongside biblical accounts of strengthening Jerusalem and using houses in defensive work.
nodes.limit: The wall bears no royal inscription. Linking its construction to one king or a particular emergency is an interpretation, and Jerusalem's construction chronology continues to be reassessed.
nodes.dateBasis: The university account assigns it to the late eighth century; the broader century bracket avoids treating attribution to Hezekiah as an inscribed date.

nodes.title: Tell es-Safi/Gath destruction layer
nodes.place: Tell es-Safi, identified with Philistine Gath
nodes.summary: An extensive destruction horizon at Gath can be compared with the biblical report of Hazael's attack.
nodes.observation: Macro- and microarchaeological study documents violent destruction and burning across excavated structures at the site.
nodes.connection: The excavators consider Hazael of Damascus the most probable historical agent, corresponding to the attack on Gath in Kings.
nodes.limit: The destruction layer does not carry the attacker's name. Linking it to Hazael combines archaeological dating, regional history, and the biblical report.
nodes.dateBasis: The primary study dates the destruction to the middle or later ninth century BCE; the range is a period bracket, not a precisely measured attack date.

nodes.title: Lachish siege ramp and battlefield remains
nodes.place: Southwestern defenses of Tel Lachish, Judah
nodes.summary: The surviving siege ramp provides archaeological evidence at the city depicted in Sennacherib's palace reliefs.
nodes.observation: A large stone ramp approaches Lachish's defenses. Archaeological and photogrammetric analysis reconstructs its construction and possible use by siege equipment.
nodes.connection: The battlefield installation can be compared with the Assyrian reliefs and biblical placement of Sennacherib at Lachish, bringing different kinds of evidence into dialogue.
nodes.limit: Detailed labor estimates and construction sequences are modern models. The physical ramp and the palace images are separate evidence, but their interpretations are not wholly independent.
nodes.dateBasis: The ramp is associated with the Assyrian assault of 701 BCE; reconstruction models should not be confused with directly recorded work schedules.

nodes.title: Ekron royal temple dedication
nodes.status: Site and ruler identified; biblical individuals distinguished
nodes.summary: A temple dedication explicitly names Ekron and its ruling family, anchoring the identification of the excavated city.
nodes.observation: The five-line inscription records a sanctuary built by Akish, son of Padi, ruler of Ekron, and invokes the blessing of a divine lady.
nodes.connection: Ekron is a Philistine city named in Kings and the prophets. The inscription identifies the archaeological site and supplies local evidence of its royal cult.
nodes.limit: The seventh-century Akish should not be equated with David's much earlier Achish of Gath. The goddess's name and identification remain disputed.
nodes.dateBasis: The inscription is assigned to the seventh century BCE; it is later than the narrative setting of David's encounters with Achish.

nodes.title: Cyrus, king of Persia
nodes.summary: Cyrus is named in the Bible and in his own Babylonian royal inscription.
nodes.observation: The Cyrus Cylinder, British Museum 90920, names the Persian conqueror of Babylon. Its royal account presents his ancestry, kingship, and restoration work.
nodes.connection: Ezra names Cyrus as king of Persia; Isaiah also addresses him by name. The cylinder supplies a surviving royal record of that ruler.
nodes.limit: The cylinder is a Babylonian proclamation. Its wording and the Jerusalem decree quoted in Ezra are separate texts; both can be followed through the linked records.

nodes.summary: The Darius named in the rebuilding period is recorded in the monumental inscription at Bisotun.

nodes.connection: Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah use Darius’s reign to date events in Jerusalem. The monument records the same Persian king’s accession and struggles for control.
nodes.limit: This entry concerns Darius I in the Persian rebuilding period. Daniel’s separately designated Darius the Mede requires its own identification discussion.

nodes.title: Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon
nodes.place: Babylon, Mesopotamia; probable origin of the selected cylinder

discovery.label: The Met purchased cylinder 86.11.60 in 1886. Its catalogue gives Babylon as a probable origin; no excavation date is assigned.

nodes.summary: Nebuchadnezzar is named throughout the exile narratives and in surviving Babylonian building inscriptions.
nodes.observation: Metropolitan Museum cylinder 86.11.60 records Nebuchadnezzar II’s construction of Babylon’s outer wall. His name and titles also appear on stamped building bricks.
nodes.connection: Kings, Jeremiah, and Daniel name this Babylonian king. His own construction record gives readers an additional written occurrence of his royal identity.
nodes.limit: Nebuchadrezzar and Nebuchadnezzar are biblical forms of the name. The museum marks the selected cylinder’s Babylon provenance as probable.
nodes.dateBasis: The museum dates the object approximately 604–562 BCE, within the king’s reign; this is not a precisely dated construction year.

nodes.title: Ahasuerus / Xerxes I, king of Persia
nodes.place: Persian Empire; Susa suggested for the vase, with exact provenance unknown

discovery.label: Louvre AO 2634 was purchased in 1895. The catalogue suggests Susa with a question mark and supplies no excavation date.

nodes.summary: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew name associated with Xerxes, whose royal name survives on multilingual inscriptions.
nodes.observation: Louvre vase AO 2634 names Xerxes I in Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian, and Egyptian royal inscriptions.
nodes.connection: Esther names Ahasuerus; Ezra places Ahasuerus between Darius and Artaxerxes. The Hebrew and Persian forms are connected in the scholarly study of the name.
nodes.limit: The name comparison follows the Hebrew text. Greek Esther calls its ruler Artaxerxes, a textual difference discussed in the linked name study.
nodes.dateBasis: The Louvre dates this vase to Xerxes’s reign, 486–465 BCE. The date refers to the surviving royal object.

recordExcerpts.note: The Louvre’s French rendering of the three cuneiform versions: Xerxes, Great King.

nodes.title: Belshazzar in a Babylonian royal inscription
aliases: Belshazzar in a Babylonian royal inscription

discovery.label: The attesting text survives in cylinders from Ur, including British Museum 91128. An individual recovery year is not assigned from the selected catalogue.

nodes.summary: An inscription commissioned by Nabonidus explicitly names Belshazzar, the royal figure named in Daniel.
nodes.observation: The Ur foundation inscription closes with a prayer for Nabonidus and his eldest son Belshazzar. CDLI identifies BM 91128 as exemplar 4 of Nabonidus 32.
nodes.connection: Daniel 5:1 names Belshazzar. The cylinder provides a non-biblical occurrence of his name within the Babylonian royal family.
nodes.limit: Daniel calls Belshazzar king; this inscription calls him Nabonidus’s eldest son. These designations are retained in their own wording.
nodes.dateBasis: The translation’s introduction proposes approximately 540 BCE for the building inscription. CDLI assigns the physical exemplar to the broader Neo-Babylonian period.

nodes.title: Tirhakah / Taharqa, king of Kush

discovery.label: The sphinx was excavated in Temple T at Kawa by the Oxford Excavation Committee. Its museum registration is 1932,0611.1; no exact excavation year is assigned here.

nodes.summary: The king called Tirhakah in Kings and Isaiah appears as Taharqa on monuments from Kush and Egypt.
nodes.observation: The British Museum’s sphinx from Kawa carries Taharqa’s name in a cartouche on its chest.
nodes.connection: Kings and Isaiah name Tirhakah as king of Kush, rendered Ethiopia in the KJV. The monument preserves this ruler’s Egyptian royal name.
nodes.limit: Taharqa’s accession is normally dated to 690 BCE. His title and role in the biblical account associated with the 701 BCE crisis are discussed in the linked chronological study.
nodes.dateBasis: The museum presentation dates the sphinx around 680 BCE, during Taharqa’s kingship. This is an object date rather than a date for the biblical episode.

nodes.title: Jerusalem
nodes.dateLabel: Late Iron Age city · 7th–early 6th centuries BCE
nodes.place: Jerusalem; southeastern ridge above the Kidron Valley

discovery.label: Yigal Shiloh's City of David excavations, 1978–1985, form one major campaign in a much longer history of research.

nodes.summary: Jerusalem's ancient urban remains occupy ridges and slopes beneath and beside the later city.
nodes.observation: Excavations on the southeastern ridge exposed domestic buildings, seal impressions and destruction deposits from the final kingdom of Judah.
nodes.connection: Second Samuel, Kings, and Luke name Jerusalem in different periods. Its archaeological remains can be explored across the city’s successive phases.
nodes.limit: The city's boundaries changed through time. The southeastern ridge lies beyond today's Old City walls, and these selected remains belong to later Judah.
nodes.dateBasis: The selected phase is the final Iron Age city, represented by dwellings destroyed in 587/586 BCE; this is not Jerusalem's foundation date.

nodes.title: Babylon
nodes.place: Babylon, near Hillah, Iraq; south of Baghdad

discovery.label: Investigated by successive archaeological missions since the nineteenth century; UNESCO's documentation distinguishes excavation, conservation and later rebuilding.

nodes.summary: Babylon's ruins preserve the monumental capital beside the Euphrates associated with Judah's exile.
nodes.observation: Walls, gateways, palaces and sacred precincts preserve the layout of the Neo-Babylonian capital, much of which remains unexcavated.
nodes.connection: Kings, Jeremiah, and Daniel name Babylon in their accounts of Judah’s exile. The archaeological site preserves the city behind those place references.
nodes.limit: Ancient foundations and later reconstruction coexist. The date range describes the Neo-Babylonian remains, within a much longer settlement history.
nodes.dateBasis: UNESCO identifies the principal visible archaeological phase with the Neo-Babylonian Empire, 626–539 BCE.

nodes.title: Nineveh
nodes.place: Eastern bank of the Tigris, within modern Mosul, Iraq

discovery.label: Excavation and re-excavation have investigated city gates and the Kuyunjik palace complex; Nebi Yunus forms another major mound within the city.

nodes.summary: Nineveh survives as a large Assyrian urban site with palace mounds, gates and an extensive circuit of defenses.
nodes.observation: Kuyunjik contains Sennacherib's palace, while Nebi Yunus marks the imperial arsenal area. The city walls extend for more than twelve kilometers.
nodes.connection: Jonah is directed to Nineveh by name, and Nahum addresses the same city. Its identified Assyrian ruins give these references a geographical setting.
nodes.limit: Kuyunjik is one mound within Nineveh, not the entire city. The selected dates describe its imperial-capital phase; occupation extended beyond that period.
nodes.dateBasis: Iraq's official nomination describes Nineveh's establishment as Sennacherib's capital around 700 BCE and its destruction in 612 BCE.

nodes.title: Ur

discovery.label: Leonard Woolley directed the joint British Museum–Penn Museum excavations from 1922 to 1934; the expedition records preserve research documentation.

nodes.summary: Southern Mesopotamian Ur preserves a Sumerian city traditionally associated with the Ur named in Genesis.
nodes.observation: The ziggurat built under Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE is one prominent surviving element of a city also investigated through houses, tombs and written records.
nodes.connection: Genesis names Ur of the Chaldees as the departure point for Terah’s household; Nehemiah recalls that origin. Southern Ur is the traditional identification used here.
nodes.limit: The archaeological identification of Sumerian Ur and its traditional association with Genesis's Ur are distinct questions. The ziggurat's date is not a date for Abraham.
nodes.dateBasis: Penn Museum's site documentation dates Ur-Nammu's ziggurat to about 2100 BCE; this point selects that monument's phase.

nodes.title: Megiddo
nodes.place: Tel Megiddo, overlooking the Jezreel Valley and the Wadi Ara route

discovery.label: Schumacher excavated in 1903–1905; the University of Chicago worked from 1925, followed by further university expeditions.

nodes.summary: Megiddo is an excavated settlement mound commanding a major route into the Jezreel Valley.
nodes.observation: Its Iron Age layers contain palaces, fortifications, large public buildings and an underground water system.
nodes.connection: First Kings names Megiddo alongside Hazor and Gezer in a list of Solomon's building projects.
nodes.limit: The identification of the site is established, while the dating and royal attribution of particular palaces and other structures remain debated.
nodes.dateBasis: The park guide discusses tenth- versus ninth-century palace dates and eighth-century urban remains; the range covers those Iron Age phases.

nodes.title: Hazor
nodes.dateLabel: Late Bronze Age city · 13th-century BCE destruction phase
nodes.place: Tel Hazor, Hula Valley, northern Galilee

discovery.label: Large-scale excavations began under Yigael Yadin in 1955; the Hebrew University expedition renewed work in 1990.

nodes.summary: Hazor preserves a large Bronze Age city and a later, smaller Iron Age settlement.
nodes.observation: The Bronze Age city comprised an upper mound and a lower enclosure. Excavated palatial remains show a major conflagration in the thirteenth century BCE.
nodes.connection: Joshua names Hazor and describes its prominence among the northern kingdoms; the archaeological site preserves the city's extensive urban footprint.
nodes.limit: The lower city belonged to Bronze Age Hazor and was not resettled with the Iron Age upper city. Different visible structures therefore represent different phases.
nodes.dateBasis: The selected century is the park guide's date for destruction of the Canaanite palace, not the foundation or total occupation of Hazor.

nodes.title: Beersheba
nodes.dateLabel: Iron Age fortified city · 9th–8th centuries BCE
nodes.place: Tel Beer Sheva, east of modern Beersheba, near the Beer Sheva and Hebron streambeds

discovery.label: Tel Aviv University excavated the mound in 1969–1976 under Yohanan Aharoni and, in the final season, Ze'ev Herzog.

nodes.summary: Tel Beer Sheva preserves the planned Iron Age town associated with biblical Beersheba.
nodes.observation: Excavations exposed gates, fortifications, houses, storehouses and water works; substantial portions of the final fortified town can be traced.
nodes.connection: Genesis names Beer-sheba in the ancestral narratives; Amos names it among later places of religious pilgrimage. The site gives the southern place-name a geographical setting.
nodes.limit: The exposed fortified urban plan belongs to the Iron Age. Genesis places its naming story in an earlier ancestral setting, and the regional name extends beyond the mound.
nodes.dateBasis: The official guide assigns fortified-city strata 5–4 to the ninth century BCE and strata 3–2 to the eighth.

nodes.title: Jericho
nodes.dateLabel: Middle Bronze Age fortified city · around 2000–1550 BCE
nodes.place: Tell es-Sultan, northwest of present-day Jericho, beside 'Ain es-Sultan in the Jordan Valley

discovery.label: Successive excavations distinguish numerous settlement phases; Italian-Palestinian expedition publications correlate their sequence with earlier investigations.

nodes.summary: Tell es-Sultan is the mound of ancient Jericho, beside the spring that sustained its settlement.
nodes.observation: Middle Bronze Age ramparts surround the remains of a substantial Canaanite town; the tell also contains much earlier Neolithic buildings.
nodes.connection: Joshua names Jericho at the beginning of its siege narrative. Tell es-Sultan identifies the ancient settlement's location.
nodes.limit: Jericho's wall systems belong to different phases. The famous Neolithic tower is millennia earlier than the Middle Bronze Age city selected here.
nodes.dateBasis: The Italian-Palestinian expedition's published sequence assigns Sultan IV's Middle Bronze Age phases to approximately 2000/1950–1550 BCE.

nodes.title: Susa / Shushan
nodes.place: Susa/Shush, southwestern Iran, beside the Shavur River

discovery.label: More than 150 years of archaeological investigation have exposed the city; the Louvre records Apadana material from the Dieulafoy mission of 1884–1886.

nodes.summary: Susa's archaeological mounds preserve the Persian royal city named in Esther.
nodes.observation: The Apadana and palace complex retain the layout of a monumental royal residence; excavated column capitals document its architectural decoration.
nodes.connection: Esther and Nehemiah name Shushan, the KJV form of Susa. Daniel 8 also names Shushan in the setting of its vision. The archaeological mounds preserve this Persian royal city.
nodes.limit: The site contains many periods. This date range selects Darius I's palace architecture rather than assigning every surviving structure to Esther's narrative setting.
nodes.dateBasis: The Louvre dates the Apadana capital AOD 1 to Darius I, 522–486 BCE, and records its palace findspot.

nodes.title: Tyre
nodes.place: Modern Sur, southern coast of Lebanon; former island and mainland Al-Bass zone

discovery.label: Lebanese and Spanish teams have researched Tyre since 1997; current international work includes the ancient island's acropolis.

nodes.summary: Tyre survives beneath and around modern Sur, with archaeological zones on its former island and mainland approaches.
nodes.observation: Al-Bass preserves a monumental road, necropolis, aqueduct and a second-century triumphal arch and hippodrome.
nodes.connection: Kings names Hiram as king of Tyre, Ezekiel addresses the city, and Acts names it as a port visited by Paul. These references lead to the coastal site beside modern Sur.
nodes.limit: The former island is now a promontory. The highlighted second-century monuments postdate the visit in Acts; earlier occupation survives beneath later urban layers.
nodes.dateBasis: UNESCO explicitly dates the Al-Bass triumphal arch and hippodrome to the second century CE.

nodes.title: The ossuary attributed to Caiaphas

discovery.label: Tomb uncovered during work in Jerusalem's Peace Forest in 1990.

nodes.summary: A decorated burial box bears a Joseph-and-Caiaphas name combination; identifying its occupant with the Gospel high priest remains disputed.
nodes.observation: The Jerusalem tomb contained several ossuaries. Two inscriptions on an ornate box name Joseph and a family name commonly read as Caiaphas; it held remains of multiple people.
nodes.connection: The Israel Museum identifies the box with the high priest associated with Jesus' interrogation. The name combination makes this a candidate connection to a named Gospel figure.
nodes.limit: Letter readings, the form of the family name and the absence of a high-priestly title leave the identification contested. The box records no trial or action involving Jesus.
nodes.dateBasis: Coins and script place the burial assemblage in the first century CE. Caiaphas's priestly tenure is not the manufacture date of the box.

nodes.title: Yehohanan's pierced heel bone

discovery.label: Excavated in a rock-cut tomb at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in 1968.

nodes.summary: A nail through a heel bone provides direct evidence of Roman crucifixion and subsequent burial in a Jerusalem family tomb.
nodes.observation: The ossuary named Yehohanan contained a right heel bone pierced by an iron nail. Its tomb context places this crucified individual within first-century Jewish burial practice.
nodes.connection: It supplies physical evidence for the kind of execution described in the Passion accounts and demonstrates that at least one crucified person received family burial.
nodes.limit: These are Yehohanan's remains, not Jesus'. One burial cannot establish how frequently Romans released bodies, and the surviving bone does not determine every detail of crucifixion technique.
nodes.dateBasis: The museum identifies the object as Herodian; the scholarly discussion dates the tomb context to the first century CE, without a secure execution year.

nodes.title: The Temple boundary warning

discovery.label: Jerusalem fragment; the consulted museum record does not supply its discovery year.

nodes.summary: A surviving Greek warning makes the Temple's restricted boundary visible in the material record.
nodes.observation: The Israel Museum's limestone fragment belongs to a warning sign prohibiting foreigners from crossing the sanctuary boundary and threatening death for violations.
nodes.connection: Acts describes an accusation that Paul brought a Greek into the Temple. The inscription independently documents the access restriction that makes that accusation intelligible.
nodes.limit: It does not name Paul or Trophimus, establish that the accusation was true, or prove a particular interpretation of the dividing-wall metaphor in Ephesians.
nodes.dateBasis: The museum dates this fragment to the Herodian period, first century BCE; the inscription remained relevant to the Temple before its destruction in 70 CE.

nodes.title: The Theodotos synagogue inscription

discovery.label: Found in a cistern south of Jerusalem's Temple Mount; no single discovery year used here.

nodes.summary: A synagogue dedication explicitly connects a Jerusalem assembly with reading the law, teaching and accommodation for visitors.
nodes.observation: The Greek text names Theodotos, a priest and synagogue leader, and describes a building for instruction, with guest rooms and water installations for travelers.
nodes.connection: It independently documents synagogue leadership and teaching practices resembling those in Luke–Acts, while showing that a synagogue could operate in Jerusalem alongside the Temple.
nodes.limit: It cannot securely identify the synagogue of the Freedmen in Acts. Its functions and date do not establish the wording or composition date of any New Testament book.
nodes.dateBasis: The scholarly edition dates the text before 70 CE; Posen places the usual paleographic attribution in the late first century BCE or early first century CE.

nodes.title: The pools in the Siloam area
nodes.dateLabel: Early Roman / late Second Temple period

discovery.label: Large stepped basin exposed in 2004; neighboring pools had earlier excavation histories.

nodes.summary: Excavated pools anchor the Siloam water landscape, while scholars differ over which basin carried the ancient name.
nodes.observation: Archaeology documents several neighboring Early Roman pools. The large stepped pool uncovered in 2004 is often called Siloam; a 2023 study instead identifies it as Solomon's Pool.
nodes.connection: The water installations establish the physical urban setting behind John's reference to Siloam. Comparing the basins and historical descriptions is necessary before assigning the Gospel name.
nodes.limit: The larger pool's identification and purpose remain interpretive questions. A pool can establish a plausible setting without demonstrating the healing narrated in John 9.
nodes.dateBasis: The date range is an orientation bracket for the late Second Temple / Early Roman installations, not a single construction date shared by all pools.

nodes.title: Magdala's synagogue and carved stone

discovery.label: Synagogue discovered in the IAA's 2009 salvage excavation; campaigns continued through 2013.

nodes.summary: A synagogue with benches, mosaics and a menorah-carved stone illuminates Jewish communal life beside the Sea of Galilee.
nodes.observation: IAA excavations recovered a synagogue with multiple construction phases. A decorated stone bearing a seven-branched menorah stood in its principal room, amid painted walls and mosaic remains.
nodes.connection: The complex supplies a local comparison for Gospel descriptions of Galilean synagogues and the region associated with Mary Magdalene.
nodes.limit: No inscription identifies Mary or records a visit by Jesus. Individual features have different dates; the stone's exact function and imagery require interpretation.
nodes.dateBasis: The 2013 report dates underlying construction to the mid-first century BCE and synagogue use to later phases. It records a 43 CE coin beneath the mosaic and an 80 CE coin in collapse.

nodes.title: The ancient Galilee boat

discovery.label: Found near Ginosar in January 1986 after the lake level fell.

nodes.summary: A conserved wooden boat reveals the scale and construction of watercraft operating on the Gospel landscape's lake.
nodes.observation: The hull, approximately eight metres long, survived in shoreline mud near Ginosar. Its timbers and associated finds have been studied and conserved since its discovery during low water.
nodes.connection: It provides a material comparison for the boats used in Gospel fishing and lake-crossing scenes.
nodes.limit: Nothing identifies an owner or connects this vessel to Jesus or a named disciple. The broad dating range is not evidence for a particular Gospel voyage.
nodes.dateBasis: The museum describes an approximately 2,000-year-old vessel; the Archaeological Institute of America dates it to the first century BCE–first century CE.

nodes.title: The village beneath later Capernaum

discovery.label: Successive excavations and reanalysis across the twentieth century; no single discovery event.

nodes.summary: Domestic remains illuminate first-century Capernaum; its famous standing limestone synagogue belongs to a much later phase.
nodes.observation: Excavation and architectural study distinguish the early village's houses and working life from the monumental synagogue and churches constructed in late antiquity.
nodes.connection: This is the settlement context of Gospel accounts placing Jesus and Peter at Capernaum. Domestic archaeology offers evidence for the community's material environment.
nodes.limit: The conspicuous white synagogue cannot simply be labeled the building in which Jesus taught. Identifying earlier basalt remains as that synagogue, or a house as Peter's, requires further inference.
nodes.dateBasis: This node is positioned at the first-century occupation discussed in the archaeological survey. The limestone synagogue is generally dated centuries later, with its precise chronology debated.

nodes.title: A coin naming Herod the tetrarch

discovery.label: Coin type represented by catalogued specimens; no single excavated findspot or discovery year assigned.

nodes.summary: A dated coin type names Herod as tetrarch and places his coinage at Tiberias.
nodes.observation: RPC I 4923 records a copper-alloy issue with Herod's tetrarch title and regnal year 33, a palm branch, and Tiberias named within a wreath.
nodes.connection: The ruler and title correspond to Herod Antipas's place in Luke's political setting. Coinage is direct contemporary evidence of his governmental identity.
nodes.limit: The type does not record John the Baptist, Jesus, or the hearing described in Luke 23. A ruler's attestation cannot establish every narrative involving him.
nodes.dateBasis: Roman Provincial Coinage converts regnal year 33 to 29/30 CE; the date is the coin issue, not the start of Antipas's reign.

nodes.title: An Early Roman dwelling at Nazareth

discovery.label: Rescue excavation reported in 2009; final settlement study published in 2020.

nodes.summary: Published excavation documents domestic occupation at Nazareth across the period in which the Gospels place Jesus' upbringing.
nodes.observation: A dwelling near the Annunciation compound contained a multilevel system of subterranean pits or silos. Pottery and stratigraphy place its main ancient phase in the late Hellenistic–Early Roman period.
nodes.connection: The excavation provides material evidence for a settlement at Nazareth during the relevant period and a comparison for local household life.
nodes.limit: It is not an identified home of Jesus or Mary. A domestic structure and its pottery establish occupation, not an individual's residence or an annunciation event.
nodes.dateBasis: Alexandre dates Stratum II to the late second century BCE–first third of the second century CE. Numerical bounds are approximate century brackets.

nodes.title: Herod's harbor at Caesarea

discovery.label: Harbor studied through repeated terrestrial and underwater campaigns; no single discovery year.

nodes.summary: Submerged breakwaters and the planned port city make Caesarea's maritime role tangible.
nodes.observation: Herod constructed an artificial harbor with substantial breakwaters, alongside a new coastal city. Archaeological study identifies hydraulic concrete technology used to build in the sea.
nodes.connection: This built environment anchors the port and administrative setting repeatedly named in Acts, including Paul's arrivals and transfer to Caesarea.
nodes.limit: The harbor does not establish a specific voyage, identify Paul's detention room or verify speeches attributed to governors. Later modifications must be separated from Herod's original works.
nodes.dateBasis: The parks authority describes a twelve-year project inaugurated in 10 BCE; research dates construction approximately 22–10/9 BCE.

nodes.title: Ephesus: theater, harbor and Artemis

discovery.label: Extensively investigated across multiple archaeological campaigns.

nodes.summary: Ephesus preserves the urban setting of a major port and cult center, including the theater named in Acts.
nodes.observation: Excavation has exposed a large theater and Roman cityscape, with harbor remains and the much-reduced site of the Temple of Artemis.
nodes.connection: These remains situate Acts' account of the Ephesian crowd and Artemis cult within an independently documented city. Revelation addresses a community in the same urban center.
nodes.limit: Physical monuments do not demonstrate the riot itself. Buildings underwent successive phases, and the later Celsus Library or Christian basilicas must not be presented as Paul's surroundings.
nodes.dateBasis: The range represents Hellenistic and Roman phases of a long-lived city, not the construction date of every surviving monument.

nodes.title: Roman Corinth and its public platform

discovery.label: Documented through long-running American School excavations; no single discovery event assigned.

nodes.summary: The excavated Roman forum includes a public speaking platform often connected with Paul's appearance before Gallio.
nodes.observation: After the colony's refoundation in 44 BCE, Roman Corinth developed a forum, temples and civic buildings. A rostra platform stood south of the forum's center.
nodes.connection: The platform is a plausible candidate for the bema in Acts 18, while the excavated colony provides a broader setting for the Corinthian correspondence.
nodes.limit: The structure does not inscribe Paul's hearing or identify its participants. Its identification with the particular tribunal in Acts remains an inference from location and function.
nodes.dateBasis: The starting date marks the Roman colony's refoundation. The broad end bracket accommodates the forum's early Imperial development and second-century additions.

nodes.title: Philippi's Roman colonial landscape

discovery.label: A continuously known monumental site investigated through successive excavations.

nodes.summary: Philippi's excavated civic landscape reflects the Roman colony described in Acts.
nodes.observation: The city was transformed after the battle of 42 BCE into a Roman colony, with a forum and monumental public buildings added to its older Hellenistic plan.
nodes.connection: This colonial setting supplies context for Acts' references to civic magistrates, public punishment and Roman citizenship, and for the destination of Philippians.
nodes.limit: The later basilicas document subsequent Christianity, not a first-century church building. Archaeology does not securely identify the jailer's house, Lydia's baptism spot or the narrated earthquake.
nodes.dateBasis: The range tracks Roman colonial development rather than one building campaign. Major surviving Christian monuments belong to later centuries and are excluded from the first-century claim.

nodes.title: Early Roman rebuilding at Sardis

discovery.label: 2015 excavation report builds on several seasons in Fields 49 and 55.

nodes.summary: Excavated Roman occupation grounds Sardis in a city that rebuilt and changed long before its surviving late-antique monuments.
nodes.observation: Field 49 preserves early Roman rebuilding, tentatively connected with the earthquake of 17 CE. The neighboring terrace held an Imperial-cult sanctuary before later reuse.
nodes.connection: The remains supply a civic and religious setting for the church addressed in Revelation, without depending on later pilgrimage buildings.
nodes.limit: The earthquake association is the excavator's proposal. Later destruction deposits and the famous synagogue cannot be treated as evidence of the congregation's spiritual condition or fulfilled prophecy.
nodes.dateBasis: The node isolates first-century urban phases. The excavation report distinguishes these from buildings and collapse assemblages extending into the sixth and seventh centuries.

nodes.title: Laodicea's city and water system

discovery.label: Multiple excavation and restoration campaigns; no single discovery year assigned.

nodes.summary: Excavated streets, public buildings and waterworks locate Laodicea in the urban network of the Lycus valley.
nodes.observation: Archaeology exposes theaters, agoras, baths and water-distribution terminals. Pipes carried spring water from the mountains south of the city through a substantial hydraulic system.
nodes.connection: These remains ground the city named in Colossians and Revelation and invite careful study of its infrastructure alongside the letters' language.
nodes.limit: The waterworks alone do not settle the meaning of Revelation's lukewarm metaphor. Later churches and restored Roman monuments are not material proof of the first-century congregation or prophetic fulfillment.
nodes.dateBasis: The broad range represents Roman Imperial urban development; individual pipes, buildings and later Christian phases require their own stratigraphic dates.

nodes.title: Pergamon's civic and sacred landscape

discovery.label: Known ruins and repeated archaeological investigations; no single discovery event assigned.

nodes.summary: Pergamon's temples, theater and healing sanctuary preserve the complex religious landscape of a city addressed in Revelation.
nodes.observation: The acropolis and lower city contain Hellenistic monuments, Roman additions and the Asclepieion. Successive regimes reshaped civic and cultic spaces.
nodes.connection: The material landscape clarifies the urban setting of Revelation's Pergamene audience, including the prominence of public religious institutions.
nodes.limit: No surviving monument is explicitly labeled as Revelation's throne of Satan. Assigning that image uniquely to the Great Altar, imperial cult or healing sanctuary remains interpretation.
nodes.dateBasis: The range brackets Hellenistic and Roman development, not one construction episode. Major Roman monuments, including the Trajan temple, postdate the first century.

quotes.editorialNote: KJV spells the city's name Pergamos.

nodes.title: Smyrna's Roman agora

discovery.label: The provincial directorate dates the first sustained agora excavations to 1933–1941.

nodes.summary: Smyrna's agora preserves the city's public life, chiefly in a phase rebuilt after the New Testament period.
nodes.observation: The surviving state agora includes stoas, a basilica and graffiti. Most visible remains belong to rebuilding after the earthquake of 178 CE.
nodes.connection: The site identifies and contextualizes the continuing city addressed in Revelation, while showing how its public spaces developed after the letter's audience lived there.
nodes.limit: The principal surviving buildings are later than Revelation. Neither this agora nor its subsequent damage demonstrates the predicted suffering of the church or identifies its first-century meeting place.
nodes.dateBasis: The date represents the documented post-178 CE reconstruction, not Smyrna's foundation or the date of Revelation.

nodes.title: Hierapolis and its thermal landscape

discovery.label: Long-known site investigated by successive archaeological missions.

nodes.summary: Thermal installations and Roman urban remains establish Hierapolis within the regional setting named in Colossians.
nodes.observation: The site preserves baths, temples, water features, a necropolis and a theater. Rebuilding followed the earthquake of 60 CE, with major development in subsequent centuries.
nodes.connection: Hierapolis stands alongside Laodicea and Colossae in the letter's description of Epaphras's concern. Its remains anchor that regional geography.
nodes.limit: The later martyr shrine and churches do not verify Epaphras's activity or identify the first-century congregation. The imposing theater belongs to a later Roman phase.
nodes.dateBasis: The range begins with the reported 60 CE earthquake and covers Roman rebuilding. UNESCO identifies the theater as Severan and the main Christian monuments as fourth–sixth century.

nodes.title: A Thyatiran dyers' association
nodes.place: Thyatira region; inscription found at Medar

discovery.label: Recorded from the village of Medar and published by Foucart in 1887; publication is not treated as a discovery date.

nodes.summary: A guild dedication documents the textile trades and civic patronage of Thyatira's later Roman society.
nodes.observation: A marble base honors Marcus, son of Menandros, for services to the dyers and for numerous civic offices. The edition identifies it as TAM V 991.
nodes.connection: It provides a regional comparison for Lydia, the dealer in purple goods from Thyatira in Acts, and for discussion of associations in Revelation's urban setting.
nodes.limit: This inscription is later than Lydia and never names her. It does not prove her guild membership or establish that Revelation's controversy concerned this particular association.
nodes.dateBasis: The scholarly edition assigns the text to the second–third centuries CE; the full range is retained rather than assigning an invented year.

nodes.title: A coin of King Agrippa

discovery.label: A coin type with multiple catalogued specimens; no single discovery date or findspot assigned.

nodes.summary: A regnal-year coin names King Agrippa, providing a contemporary material witness to the ruler associated with Acts 12.
nodes.observation: RPC I 4981 catalogues a copper-alloy type naming King Agrippa, with a canopy, three grain ears and a year-six date.
nodes.connection: The preferred attribution is Agrippa I, the Herodian ruler conventionally identified with the king called Herod in Acts 12.
nodes.limit: The coin does not record the deaths of James or the king, Peter's imprisonment, or any miracle. RPC notes a proposed alternative attribution to Agrippa II and retains Agrippa I.
nodes.dateBasis: RPC Online dates the type to 41/42 CE and assigns it to Jerusalem; its editorial note records an alternative ruler-and-mint proposal.

nodes.title: Enuma Elish · Creation poem tablet

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: A Babylonian creation poem gives readers a neighboring ancient account of cosmic order.
nodes.observation: The seventh-century copy K.3567 belongs to the Enuma Elish tradition. The poem celebrates Marduk and describes the ordering of the heavens and the establishment of the gods’ world.
nodes.connection: It offers comparative context for Genesis’s treatment of creation, waters, and ordered time. The connection is a literary comparison, not an identification of the stories as identical.
nodes.limit: The tablet cannot establish the truth or date of Genesis 1. Its copy date must be distinguished from debated dates of the poem’s composition and any hypothesized contact between traditions.
nodes.dateBasis: Museo Galileo’s exhibition identifies K.3567 as a seventh-century BCE copy; the date of the broader composition is a separate scholarly question.

nodes.title: Gilgamesh XI · The Flood Tablet

discovery.label: Excavated at Kouyunjik in 1853 by Hormuzd Rassam.

nodes.summary: An Assyrian-period tablet preserves a Mesopotamian flood narrative for comparison with Genesis.
nodes.observation: The tablet copies part of Gilgamesh XI: a divine plan for a destructive flood, a warning to Utnapishtim, and instructions to build a boat for survival.
nodes.connection: It supplies an ancient literary comparison for Noah’s story. Similar themes invite study of shared narrative traditions and of the differences between the accounts.
nodes.limit: This is a Mesopotamian literary witness, not geological evidence for a worldwide flood or independent identification of Noah. The tablet’s date is not the first composition date of Gilgamesh.
nodes.dateBasis: Getty’s object record identifies a seventh-century BCE Neo-Assyrian copy and an 1853 excavation at Kouyunjik.

nodes.title: Atra-hasis · Babylonian flood fragment

discovery.label: Purchased by the Metropolitan Museum in 1886; no precise excavation context asserted.

nodes.summary: A clay fragment preserves another version of the ancient flood tradition.
nodes.observation: The Met’s tablet describes humanity’s noise and the gods’ response; its reverse preserves the story’s ending and names the survivor Utnapishtim. The museum identifies it with the Atra-hasis tradition.
nodes.connection: It provides comparative material for the causes, survival, and aftermath of the Genesis flood narrative. Different divine motives and theologies are part of the comparison.
nodes.limit: Shared motifs do not prove the biblical event or establish a simple one-step borrowing relationship. This is a later copy of a tradition also known from older manuscripts.
nodes.dateBasis: The museum assigns this object to about the seventh–sixth century BCE; that date concerns the tablet rather than the tradition’s origin.

nodes.title: Codex Sinaiticus
nodes.dateLabel: Usually 4th century CE; broader dating debated
nodes.place: Saint Catherine’s Monastery tradition; leaves now divided among repositories

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: In this Greek Bible, Mark ends at 16:8 and is followed by Luke.
nodes.observation: The manuscript contains the New Testament alongside surviving Greek Old Testament books, Barnabas, and the Shepherd of Hermas. The project’s folio 228 places Mark 16:1–8 immediately before Luke.
nodes.connection: It supplies actual wording for comparison across manuscripts. Its ending of Mark gives readers a concrete case in which an ancient witness differs from the longer ending printed in many Bibles.
nodes.limit: The date is a manuscript estimate, not a date of Gospel composition. This copy is not eyewitness testimony, and its extra works do not by themselves define every ancient community’s canon.
nodes.dateBasis: Palaeography and manuscript features usually support a fourth-century attribution; Nongbri’s 2022 study argues for an early-fourth to early-fifth-century possibility range.

nodes.title: Codex Vaticanus

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: The ancient portion of this Greek Bible preserves Hebrews through 9:13; later writing supplies the continuation.
nodes.observation: The ancient New Testament portion preserves the Gospels, Acts, letters, and Hebrews through 9:13. The catalog distinguishes the later writing that follows from the fourth-century material.
nodes.connection: It makes many early Greek readings directly inspectable and comparable with papyri such as P75. The listed biblical passages indicate surviving textual coverage.
nodes.limit: The surviving ancient portion lacks the Pastorals, Philemon, and Revelation. Later replacement material must not be dated automatically to the original copying campaign.
nodes.dateBasis: Fourth-century palaeographic attribution in the manuscript catalog; not a dated autograph.

nodes.title: Codex Alexandrinus · Greek Bible
nodes.dateLabel: First half of the 5th century CE
nodes.place: British Library · Royal MS 1 D V–VIII

discovery.label: Reached England as a royal gift in 1627; not an archaeological discovery.

nodes.summary: A fifth-century Greek Bible preserves Genesis through Chronicles, including Ruth, with some missing material.
nodes.observation: British Library volume 1 catalogs Genesis through Chronicles, including Ruth and the books called Kingdoms in Greek. The wider codex also preserves New Testament material and the Clementine writings, with losses.
nodes.connection: The selected passages show the transmission of Genesis, Ruth, and the monarchy narratives in Greek. Readers can distinguish a translation witness from a Hebrew manuscript.
nodes.limit: The codex has missing leaves and textual gaps. Its fifth-century production does not date the Hebrew books’ composition or independently verify their narratives.
nodes.dateBasis: The British Library’s scholarly account places copying probably in the first half of the fifth century.

nodes.title: Codex Bezae

discovery.label: Presented to Cambridge by Theodore Beza in 1581.

nodes.summary: Greek and Latin Gospel and Acts texts appear on facing pages in this parchment codex.
nodes.observation: The parchment codex places Greek beside Latin. Cambridge’s catalog documents surviving passages, replacement leaves, corrections, and a text of Acts that differs markedly from other witnesses.
nodes.connection: It allows comparison of two language traditions and illustrates that textual transmission includes meaningful variation, not only spelling differences.
nodes.limit: Greek and Latin sides are not always identical, and many passages are incomplete. The place of production remains disputed; the date does not establish the authorship of Acts.
nodes.dateBasis: Cambridge’s exhibition assigns the late fourth or fifth century; the exact origin and year remain uncertain.

nodes.title: Codex Washingtonianus · Freer Gospels
nodes.place: Egypt; Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art · F1906.274

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: This Gospel book arranges its texts in the order Matthew, John, Luke, Mark.
nodes.observation: The Freer codex contains the four Gospels in the order Matthew, John, Luke, Mark. Its surviving parchment leaves provide a separate physical witness for comparing Gospel readings.
nodes.connection: The passage labels identify its four-book scope, rather than claiming every verse survives without loss. Its order illustrates ancient book-making choices within a four-Gospel collection.
nodes.limit: Some material is missing or replaced. The manuscript is a later copy, not a record written during Jesus’s ministry, and its Egyptian association does not identify its original scribe.
nodes.dateBasis: Smithsonian dates it late fourth–early fifth century; CSNTM gives fourth–fifth century. The display bracket is approximate.

nodes.title: Aleppo Codex

discovery.label: Brought to Israel in 1958 after losses in Aleppo; not a new excavation.

nodes.summary: A medieval Hebrew Bible records the Masoretic reading tradition in exceptional detail.
nodes.observation: The Ben-Zvi project identifies this tenth-century Bible with Aaron Ben Asher’s Masoretic work. The surviving leaves include the Song of Moses and the Chronicles passage highlighted by the Israel Museum.
nodes.connection: It witnesses the consonants and accompanying reading tradition of the Hebrew Bible. Comparison with older scrolls can reveal both continuity and differences.
nodes.limit: Substantial portions are missing. Its medieval date concerns this copy and its annotations, not the first writing of Deuteronomy or Chronicles.
nodes.dateBasis: Custodial project attribution to about 930 CE; the numerical bracket is a display approximation.

nodes.title: Leningrad Codex
nodes.place: Probably Cairo/Fustat; National Library of Russia · Firkovich B 19 A

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: A complete medieval Hebrew Bible preserves the Masoretic text across all narrative stages.
nodes.observation: The codex includes the whole Hebrew Bible with vowel signs, accents, and textual notes. Its copying is associated with Samuel ben Jacob in early-eleventh-century Egypt.
nodes.connection: It provides a complete comparison point for earlier fragmentary witnesses. Its stage links indicate books whose text it preserves, including narratives many centuries older than the copy.
nodes.limit: A complete copy is not an independent archaeological confirmation of every story. The preservation of medieval wording does not eliminate earlier variants.
nodes.dateBasis: Cambridge describes completion around 1008–1009; USC rounds the date to about 1010. The labels preserve that difference rather than manufacturing an exact day.

nodes.title: Cairo Genizah · dated Nehemiah fragment

discovery.label: Donated to Cambridge in 1898 within the Taylor-Schechter Genizah Collection.

nodes.summary: A dated colophon accompanies a fragment of Nehemiah’s final chapter.

nodes.title: P45 · Gospels and Acts
nodes.place: Egyptian acquisition context; Chester Beatty and Vienna

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: A papyrus codex preserves portions of all four Gospels together with Acts.

nodes.limit: Large gaps remain. Combining books in one ancient codex is evidence of reception and transmission, not proof of their authorship or of every reported event.
nodes.dateBasis: Third-century palaeographic attribution; the displayed century is not an exact production year.

nodes.title: P46 · Letters collected on papyrus
nodes.place: Egypt; University of Michigan and Chester Beatty

discovery.label: Michigan leaves acquired in 1930–1931; precise excavation context is not securely documented here.

nodes.summary: A substantial early collection places Hebrews among letters attributed to Paul.
nodes.observation: The surviving codex preserves portions of nine letters, with Hebrews following Romans. Its opening and final leaves are missing; Michigan explains which contents are preserved and which must remain conjectural.
nodes.connection: It gives a material witness to the circulation of Pauline letters as a collection. Hebrews’ placement records a historical reception choice.
nodes.limit: The collection’s inclusion of Hebrews does not establish Paul as its author. The lost ending cannot prove whether the Pastorals or other writings were originally present.
nodes.dateBasis: Usually described as around 200 CE; the Michigan-associated catalog gives a broad late-second to early-third-century range.

nodes.title: P47 · Revelation on papyrus
nodes.place: Egyptian acquisition context; Chester Beatty · BP III

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: Ten papyrus leaves preserve an early stretch of Revelation.
nodes.observation: The catalog identifies a Greek papyrus manuscript of Revelation with ten surviving leaves. Its image index runs from material in chapter 9 to chapter 17.
nodes.connection: It witnesses the wording and copying of Revelation well before medieval codices. The chapter range marks partial survival, not an intact copy of the whole book.
nodes.limit: It does not provide an independent record of the visions’ events or settle their interpretation. Missing material limits verse-by-verse comparisons.
nodes.dateBasis: CSNTM describes the manuscript as late third century; the range is palaeographic, not a dated colophon.

quotes.text: The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ;
quotes.fullText: And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever.

nodes.title: P66 · Bodmer II, Gospel of John
nodes.dateLabel: Often around 200 CE; 4th century also proposed
nodes.place: Bodmer collection and associated fragments; precise find circumstances debated

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: A substantial papyrus witness to John survives with related fragments in several collections.
nodes.observation: The manuscript preserves Greek John. CSNTM’s public Chester Beatty images include fragmentary material from John 19; scholarship studies the larger Bodmer codex.
nodes.connection: The surviving text can be compared with later copies of John. The selected verses are verified examples, not a full inventory of its contents.
nodes.limit: Handwriting does not yield a precise year. A wider proposed date range must be kept distinct from John’s composition date and from the date of the crucifixion narrative.
nodes.dateBasis: The conventional late-second/early-third-century date is reported alongside Nongbri’s argument that fourth-century comparanda widen the possibilities; the range is not a statistical interval.

quotes.text: Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother,
quotes.fullText: Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.

nodes.title: P75 · Hanna Papyrus 1

discovery.label: Acquired for the Vatican in 2006; this is a collection transfer, not an excavation date.

nodes.summary: Luke and John survive together in a papyrus Gospel codex.
nodes.observation: The codex preserves substantial portions of Luke and John. The Vatican’s presentation reproduces the Lukan Lord’s Prayer and John’s prologue; the manuscript shares many readings with Vaticanus.
nodes.connection: It allows comparison of prayers and narrative wording across early copies. Agreement with Vaticanus is evidence about textual relationships, rather than proof of identical transmission everywhere.
nodes.limit: Its date remains debated. The manuscript’s close agreement with another copy does not determine which exemplar was used or establish the dates of Gospel composition.
nodes.dateBasis: CSNTM gives the third century. Nongbri’s 2016 analysis of handwriting and book construction argues that a fourth-century date is plausible.

quotes.text: Hallowed be thy name.

quotes.editorialNote: P75 has a shorter form of the Lord's Prayer than the KJV; display only the shared clause Hallowed be thy name. The quotation remains labeled KJV.

quotes.fullText: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

nodes.title: P90 · John fragment from Oxyrhynchus

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: A small Greek fragment preserves part of John’s trial narrative.
nodes.observation: P.Oxy. 3523 is a fragment of a papyrus Gospel manuscript. The scholarly image catalog locates its surviving text in John 18 and 19.
nodes.connection: It is another physical witness to John’s narrative of Pilate and Jesus, distinct from P52 and from the inscription naming Pilate.
nodes.limit: A copied Gospel passage is not an independent witness to the trial. The century attribution is palaeographic and should not be converted into a precise year.
nodes.dateBasis: Second-century catalog attribution based on the script; no explicit production date survives.

quotes.text: My kingdom is not of this world:
quotes.fullText: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.

nodes.title: P104 · Matthew fragment from Oxyrhynchus

discovery.label: Preserved or acquired manuscript; no excavation date is asserted in this record.

nodes.summary: A very small papyrus fragment preserves part of Matthew’s vineyard parable.
nodes.observation: P.Oxy. 4404 has writing on a fragment of a codex leaf. The image catalog identifies text beginning at Matthew 21:34 and traces associated with 21:43 on the other side.
nodes.connection: It witnesses early copying of Matthew’s parable. Even small fragments can anchor particular words to an actual material copy.
nodes.limit: The reverse is badly preserved. This record makes no firm claim about the disputed presence or absence of Matthew 21:44, and the copy does not establish when Matthew was composed.
nodes.dateBasis: Second-century palaeographic attribution in the catalog; precision within that century is not established here.

quotes.text: But last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son.
quotes.fullText: But last of all he sent unto them his son, saying, They will reverence my son.

nodes.title: 4Q41 · All Souls Deuteronomy

discovery.label: Recovered with Qumran Cave 4 manuscripts in 1952.

nodes.summary: A small Deuteronomy manuscript preserves the Decalogue in an excerpted arrangement.
nodes.observation: The manuscript contains selected Deuteronomy passages, including the commandments. Specialist Shani Tzoref notes that its Sabbath wording draws together elements from Exodus and Deuteronomy.
nodes.connection: It supplies a direct witness to biblical wording and its use. The Exodus reference marks a textual parallel, not a separately preserved complete Exodus manuscript.
nodes.limit: Its possible liturgical function is an interpretation. A first-century BCE copy of commandments does not date Sinai or establish the historicity of the Exodus.
nodes.dateBasis: First-century BCE attribution reported by the specialist discussion; modern recovery occurred in 1952.

quotes.text: Keep the sabbath day to sanctify it, as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee.
quotes.fullText: Keep the sabbath day to sanctify it, as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee.

quotes.text: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is,
quotes.fullText: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.
quotes.editorialNote: Exodus is a parallel for the harmonized Sabbath wording in this Deuteronomy witness, not a separate Exodus manuscript.

nodes.title: 11Q5 · Great Psalms Scroll

discovery.label: Found in Cave 11 in 1956; unrolled in 1961.

nodes.summary: A Psalms collection preserves familiar compositions in a different sequence.
nodes.observation: The scroll contains biblical psalms, additional hymns, and prose about David’s compositions. Its preserved sequence differs from the standard Hebrew Psalter; parts of many psalms are missing.
nodes.connection: It illuminates the collection and transmission of worship texts associated with David. The passage range identifies the main part of the Psalter represented, not uninterrupted coverage.
nodes.limit: It is much later than David and does not verify Davidic authorship. Scholars debate whether its arrangement represents a Psalter edition or a collection for another use.
nodes.dateBasis: The Library of Congress exhibition, using IAA material, dates the copy about 30–50 CE from its Herodian script.

quotes.fullText: The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that be bowed down.
quotes.editorialNote: Psalm 145:14 lies in preserved 145:13–21. https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/35006/chapter/298748365

nodes.title: 11Q1 · Paleo-Hebrew Leviticus

discovery.label: Discovered in Cave 11 in 1956; unrolled fourteen years later.

nodes.summary: An archaic Hebrew script carries a later copy of Leviticus.
nodes.observation: The main surviving piece preserves the lower parts of columns from Leviticus 22–27. Additional fragments belong to earlier chapters; dots separate words in the paleo-Hebrew writing.
nodes.connection: It provides a physical witness to Leviticus alongside copies written in other scripts. The script’s archaic appearance is distinct from the manuscript’s actual production period.
nodes.limit: The scroll is fragmentary and belongs to the Second Temple period. Paleo-Hebrew letters do not make it a manuscript from the wilderness generation.
nodes.dateBasis: The Library of Congress / IAA exhibition dates copying to the late second or early first century BCE; the numerical range is approximate.

collections.title: The Context of Scripture Online
collections.institution: Brill · William W. Hallo and K. Lawson Younger Jr., editors
collections.scope: A broad, four-volume collection of ancient Near Eastern literary compositions, monumental inscriptions, archival documents, and supplementary texts.
collections.use: Start here to identify published editions and cross-cultural comparisons across the Hebrew Bible’s world.
collections.limit: A table-of-contents entry is a research lead, not a finding verified in this collection. Translations and commentary may require institutional access.
collections.access: Public text index reviewed; individual subscription texts have not all been read.

collections.title: ORACC · Royal inscriptions and ancient archives
collections.scope: Linked scholarly projects include Assyrian and Babylonian royal inscriptions, state archives, and annotated cuneiform editions.
collections.use: Trace rulers, places, campaigns, and administrative language through editions rather than popular summaries.
collections.limit: Several exemplars can preserve an inscription. Record each physical witness and link it to the shared composition and other catalogues.
collections.access: Public project descriptions reviewed; availability of individual project servers varies.

collections.title: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative
collections.scope: A large catalog of cuneiform objects with identifiers, collection information, images, and text data where available.
collections.use: Resolve an object’s identity and provenance, and connect museum numbers with editions and photographs.
collections.limit: Entries cover many periods, places, and languages. Follow the object identifier to the available photograph, transliteration, and publication history.
collections.access: Project description reviewed; open online catalog.

collections.title: Hebrew Inscriptions: Texts from the Biblical Period of the Monarchy
collections.institution: F. W. Dobbs-Allsopp, J. J. M. Roberts, C. L. Seow, and R. E. Whitaker · Yale University Press, 2005
collections.scope: A major English-language philological collection of substantive Hebrew inscriptions from the Iron II period, with translations, commentary, bibliography, and concordance.
collections.use: Build out the Hebrew epigraphy register systematically, including less famous administrative and everyday documents.
collections.limit: Coverage reflects the material available to the editors; subsequent discoveries and revised readings need later publications.
collections.access: Publisher-supplied bibliographic description reviewed; full book not read in this research pass.

collections.title: Handbuch der althebräischen Epigraphik
collections.scope: A standard multi-volume reference for ancient Hebrew inscriptions; the study edition reprints the earlier work with bibliographical updating.
collections.use: Compare text editions, paleography, and linguistic analysis alongside the English Hebrew Inscriptions volume.
collections.limit: A reference edition is not a continuously updated census. Dates and restorations still require evaluation.
collections.access: Library bibliographic record reviewed; print or library access needed for the full work.

collections.title: Hebrew Stamp Seals
collections.institution: Scholarly database identified in Cambridge’s Ancient Hebrew Inscriptions
collections.scope: A specialist database of provenanced Iron Age Paleo-Hebrew seals and seal impressions.
collections.use: Expand official-name and administrative evidence while giving documented find contexts priority.
collections.limit: Name, patronymic, office, date, and excavation context are useful search fields for following personal-name connections.
collections.access: Scope verified through the scholarly Cambridge guide; the database itself was not accessible to the research tool.

collections.title: Ancient Near Eastern Texts Relating to the Old Testament
collections.institution: James B. Pritchard, editor · Princeton University Press
collections.scope: An influential anthology of historical, legal, religious, and literary texts used for comparison with the Hebrew Bible.
collections.use: Follow the older ANET references frequently cited in archaeological and biblical scholarship.
collections.limit: Translations reflect the editions available to the contributors. Follow the publication references and later readings alongside each selected text.
collections.access: JSTOR book description reviewed; full-text access depends on entitlement.

collections.title: Corpus Inscriptionum Iudaeae/Palaestinae
collections.institution: International scholarly project · De Gruyter Brill
collections.scope: A comprehensive multilingual publication project for inscriptions of the region from Alexander’s era through the end of Byzantine rule.
collections.use: Find critical editions for Jewish, Greek, Latin, and other inscriptions relevant to the Gospels and later communities.
collections.limit: Most of its chronological range extends beyond New Testament events. Date each inscription before making a connection.
collections.access: Publisher series description reviewed; volumes may require purchase or library access.

collections.title: Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine
collections.institution: Ancient Inscriptions from Israel / Palestine project
collections.scope: A digital project making inscriptions searchable and usable across an interconnected research collection.
collections.use: Locate texts and bibliographic connections, then consult the cited critical edition.
collections.limit: The digital project and CIIP can describe the same object; overlapping records should be linked, not counted twice.
collections.access: Indexed project description reviewed; direct page retrieval timed out.

collections.title: Ḥadashot Arkheologiyot · Excavations and Surveys in Israel
collections.scope: Open bilingual excavation reports: preliminary reports for larger projects and final reports for smaller excavations and surveys.
collections.use: Check stratigraphy, dated finds, and changing site interpretations against the excavators’ reports.
collections.limit: A preliminary report can change after fuller analysis. A site’s biblical identification and a structure’s date are separate questions.
collections.access: Current journal landing page and publication scope reviewed; open access.

collections.title: ISAC publications and excavation reports
collections.institution: University of Chicago · Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures
collections.scope: Research monographs, excavation reports, text editions, museum catalogs, and related publications across ancient Near Eastern cultures.
collections.use: Follow original project publications, including major excavations and inscription editions.
collections.limit: The publication catalog includes many subjects unrelated to the Bible. Individual claims require the relevant pages and dating evidence.
collections.access: Current publication catalog and institutional publication policy reviewed; many PDFs are available.

collections.title: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library
collections.scope: A digital archive of Judean Desert manuscripts searchable by site, language, content, and identifier, with historical and modern imaging.
collections.use: Expand biblical textual witnesses by manuscript and passage, recording variants as well as continuity.
collections.limit: Each fragment preserves a particular passage and physical extent. Record its copying date, reading, and links to other witnesses.
collections.access: Archive interface and description reviewed; individual records have varying descriptive detail.

collections.title: New Testament Virtual Manuscript Room
collections.institution: Institute for New Testament Textual Research · University of Münster
collections.scope: A central research environment for Greek New Testament manuscripts, with manuscript catalogs, images, transcriptions, and textual research tools.
collections.use: Identify witnesses by Gregory–Aland number, inspect surviving passages, and compare readings.
collections.limit: Use Gregory–Aland numbers to connect photographs, transcriptions, and holding libraries for the same manuscript. Image permissions vary.
collections.access: Public landing page and scope reviewed; some functions require an account.

collections.title: CSNTM manuscript library
collections.institution: Center for the Study of New Testament Manuscripts
collections.scope: A manuscript catalog and digital imaging resource for New Testament textual study.
collections.use: Locate photographs and holding-library information for witnesses selected from the manuscript register.
collections.limit: Many manuscripts also appear in NTVMR and library catalogs. Those records are different access routes to the same witness.
collections.access: Indexed catalog reviewed; image access and availability depend on the manuscript and holding institution.

collections.title: Taylor–Schechter Cairo Genizah Collection
collections.scope: A major collection of medieval Jewish manuscript fragments, including biblical, liturgical, and documentary material.
collections.use: Study later Hebrew textual transmission, reading traditions, and Jewish manuscript culture.
collections.limit: The collection includes many non-biblical documents. Medieval witnesses should not be presented as artifacts from biblical narrative periods.
collections.access: Library collection history reviewed; the page links onward to the research unit.

collections.title: Friedberg Genizah Project
collections.scope: A research platform linking Genizah images, catalog descriptions, and bibliographical references across dispersed collections.
collections.use: Reconnect fragments and follow their publications across holding institutions.
collections.limit: Images, shelfmarks, and fragments are different counting units. A fragment appearing here and at Cambridge remains one physical witness.
collections.access: Project description reviewed; research-platform access conditions may vary.

collections.title: Papyri.info
collections.scope: A portal joining published papyrus texts with catalog records, bibliography, and related resources; literary materials are also represented.
collections.use: Investigate administration, contracts, language, and everyday practices in the wider Roman world.
collections.limit: Literary and everyday documents share the portal. Use the catalogue’s date, place, language, and publication fields to explore each connection.
collections.access: Live portal and institutional description reviewed; open text access where available.

collections.title: PHI Greek Inscriptions
collections.scope: Greek inscriptions from major printed corpora, searchable by text and browsable by region and publication.
collections.use: Check civic titles, officials, cults, and places across the cities of Acts and Revelation.
collections.limit: Read editorial restorations separately from surviving letters. Texts from later centuries cannot silently stand in for first-century evidence.
collections.access: Project description and regional scope reviewed; editions are primarily in Greek.

collections.title: Epigraphic Database Heidelberg
collections.scope: Latin and bilingual epigraphic records with textual, bibliographic, photographic, and geographical data.
collections.use: Investigate Roman offices, provincial administration, and inscription parallels.
collections.limit: Names and civic titles can be searched alongside dates and findspots. Coverage and available images vary between records.
collections.access: Institutional data-reuse documentation reviewed; catalog and data-service availability can vary.

collections.title: Trismegistos
collections.institution: KU Leuven and collaborating research projects
collections.scope: An interconnected metadata resource for ancient texts, people, places, and collections across languages and writing materials.
collections.use: Reconcile identifiers and connect records that describe the same ancient document.
collections.limit: Metadata links are navigation aids, not new independent evidence. Full texts generally belong to the linked edition or collection.
collections.access: Institutional project description and public data-service documentation reviewed.

collections.title: Biblical-person identification research
collections.institution: Lawrence J. Mykytiuk · Purdue University repository / Biblical Archaeology Review
collections.scope: A documented study of 53 Hebrew Bible figures identified in inscriptions, with references and explicit identification criteria.
collections.use: Use the bibliography to find the actual inscription and evaluate matching name, patronymic, office, place, and date.
collections.limit: The study’s selection and identification criteria are the author’s. Each proposed identification can be followed back to its cited inscription.
collections.access: Repository description and linked study’s indexed documentation reviewed.

collections.title: Mari royal archives · ARM and Florilegium Marianum
collections.scope: A guide to Mari’s palace archives, approximately 20,000 tablets and fragments: correspondence, administrative records, legal documents, and other texts.
collections.use: Start with an ARM or FM publication number, then follow its edition and catalogue identifier. Selected Mari letters are linked to Genesis in this collection.
collections.limit: The overview’s publication tally is dated June 2022. Tablet fragments, reconstructed texts, and publications are different counting units.
collections.access: Public institutional overview read; the page links to the ARCHIBAB research database and publication bibliography.

collections.title: Nuzi tablets · household and family archives
collections.scope: An institutional introduction to the Nuzi tablets and the recovery and conservation of documents recording family, property, and everyday affairs.
collections.use: Follow individual HSS and JEN publication numbers into the tablet editions. HSS V 60, 67, and 72 now have their own Genesis data points.
collections.limit: This overview describes the collection. Individual dates, rooms, parties, and clauses belong in the record of each tablet.
collections.access: Harvard’s public collection report read; individual selected tablets are supported by their own editions.

collections.title: Patriarchal names in the Amorite records
collections.scope: A scholarly study comparing Genesis personal names with Amorite name forms and other ancient attestations.
collections.use: Follow a name’s transliteration and bibliography to the actual tablet or inscription; preserve each spelling and publication reference.
collections.limit: The article presents Millard’s argument and discusses other scholars’ interpretations. Its comparative name lists are a guide for finding individual records.
collections.access: Open article read in the relevant sections on name forms and their sources.

collections.title: Bible Geocoding Data
collections.scope: Geographic names, verse references, and proposed locations across the Protestant Bible, compiled from more than seventy modern reference sources.
collections.use: All 1,285 verse-linked entries from the recorded snapshot are included as data points. Follow each entry to its biblical references and the source discussion.
collections.limit: Catalogue entries can represent alternative names, textual readings, or distinct contexts. The full index retains those distinctions and proposed identifications.
collections.access: Open dataset under CC BY 4.0. Source snapshot and import provenance retained with this project.
